(p-329) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on Surat al-Nur

This surah is entirely Medinan.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear signs, that you may remember.﴾ ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes. Let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God, if you believe in God and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾

The majority of readers recited "surah" with a *raf'* (nominative). 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Mujahid recited "surah" with a *nasb* (accusative). This is also transmitted from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and from Abu al-Darda'. The *raf'* reading is the predicate of an implied subject, whose assumed form is: "This is a surah." Or it is a subject whose predicate is placed first, whose assumed form is: "In what is recited to you." It is also possible that the word "surah" is the subject, and what follows it is an adjective describing it, which removes it from being a purely indefinite noun, so the beginning with it becomes acceptable. In that case the predicate is the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man﴾ and what follows them. The meaning is: the surah that was sent down, made obligatory, such-and-such. This is because a surah is an expression for a sequence of verses that has a beginning and an end. However, this view faces the objection that the subject being the predicate is not clear, unless the predicate is taken to be the whole surah, and this is far-fetched by analogy.

(p-330) The *nasb* reading is based on an implied verb, which some assumed as: "Recite a surah," or something similar. Some made it: "We sent down a surah which We sent down." Al-Farra' said: it is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) of the pronoun (ha') and the alif (in "anzalnaha" and "faradnaha"), and a circumstantial phrase from a pronoun may precede it.

The majority of readers recited "wa faradnaha" with a light *ra'* (fara-dna). Its meaning is affirmation and obligation in its most emphatic form, since it is likened to an obligation in binding force. Mujahid and others, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, and Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, recited "wa farradnaha" with a doubled *ra'*, and its meaning is: We made them *fara'id* (obligations). Because this word is repeated, the verb is intensified for emphasis and multiplication. Al-A'mash recited "wa faradnaha lakum." Al-Zahrawi reported from some scholars that he said: everything in the surah that is a command or a prohibition is an obligation.

"The clear signs": their parables, their admonitions, and their rulings. Al-Zahrawi said: the meaning is that there is nothing in them that is ambiguous, their interpretation agrees with their outward meaning.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is arbitrary judgement.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿that you may remember﴾ mean: in the hope and expectation of people.

The majority of readers recited "al-zaniyatu" with a *raf'*. 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "al-zaniyata" with a *nasb*. According to Sibawayh, the *nasb* is more eloquent, because in his view it is like your saying: "Zaydan, I strike." The *raf'* in his view is that it is a predicate of a beginning (p-331) assumed as: "In what is recited to you, the adulterous woman and the adulterous man." The people agreed on the *raf'*, though according to Sibawayh the analogy favours the *nasb*. As for al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, the *raf'* is the more eloquent in their view, and the predicate is the words of Him, exalted is He, "flog" (fajlidu), because the meaning is: the adulterous woman and the adulterous man are flogged by the judgement of God, blessed and exalted is He. This is a good view, and it is the view of most grammarians. If you wish, you may assume the predicate to be "they should be flogged" (yanbaghi an yujlada). Ibn Mas'ud recited "wal-zan" without the *ya'*. The woman is mentioned first in the wording because at that time the fornication of women was more widespread, and the slave-girls of the Arabs and the prostitutes of the time had banners, and they were openly so. Disgrace is more severe for women, since their place is seclusion and protection, so their mention was placed first for severity and emphasis. The definite article in His words ﴿the adulterous woman and the adulterous man﴾ is generic, which indicates that it is general to all fornicators. This verse, by agreement, abrogates (naskh, i.e. the cancellation of an earlier ruling) the verse of confinement and the verse of harm in Surat al-Nisa'. The community of scholars holds that this verse is general, and that the ruling for married persons is abrogated from it. They differed over the abrogating text. One group said: the abrogating text is the mutawatir Sunnah concerning stoning. Another group said: rather, it is the Qur'an whose wording was removed but whose ruling remained, and this is what 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, recited from the pulpit in the presence of the Companions, may God be pleased with them: "The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them outright," and he said: "We recited it in the Book of God." All agreed that its wording was removed (p-332) and its ruling remained. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Rahawayh said: there is no abrogation in this verse; rather, the Sunnah of stoning came as an addition. So the married person, in the view of this group, is flogged and then stoned. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and he did it to Shurahah. Their evidence is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The married man (thayyib) with the married woman: a hundred lashes and stoning." This is refuted by the Prophet's ﷺ action, since he stoned and did not flog. The majority of the community held this view, since his action is like his saying: it removed the flogging from the married person. Ibn Salam and others said: this verse is specific to the unmarried pair (bikrayn).

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Because if nothing of this ruling remained except for the unmarried pair. They used as evidence for this the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The unmarried man with the unmarried woman: a hundred lashes and a year's exile," and his saying: "Upon your son, a hundred lashes." (p-333) They used as evidence that it is not general the exclusion of slave-girls, slaves and others from it. Much of these meanings have been expounded earlier in Surat al-Nisa'.

Flogging takes place with the flogged person seated, according to Malik, and it is not sufficient in his view except on the back. The people of opinion (Abu Hanifa and his school) and al-Shafi'i hold that the man should be flogged while standing. This is also the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. The blows are distributed over all the limbs. Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, pointed to the two legs of a slave-girl whom he flogged for fornication. The consensus is on sparing the face, the private parts, and the vital places. The view of Malik, may God have mercy on him, is preferred by the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Or a punishment upon your back," and the words of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "Or I will surely make your back ache." The man is stripped according to Malik, al-Nakha'i, Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and others, who hold that he should be struck over a shirt. This is also the view of 'Uthman and Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with them both. As for the woman, she is covered, by one opinion without dispute.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman's readings: The majority recited "ra'fah" with a silent hamza on the pattern *fa'lah*. Ibn Kathir recited "ra'fah" on the pattern *fa'alah* with an open 'ayn. 'Asim also recited "ra'afah" on the pattern *fa'alah*, like *sa'amah* and *ka'abah*. These are verbal nouns, the first of which is the most famous, from "ra'afa," when one softens and shows mercy. The majority recited "ta'khudhukum" with a *ta'* above (p-334), and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "ya'khudhukum" with a *ya'* below.

People differed about the pity that is forbidden: what is it? Abu Mijlaz, Lahiq ibn Humayd, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and 'Ata' said: it is in dropping the prescribed punishment, that is: carry it out without fail. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, and Ibn Jubayr and others. In their view, the flogging for fornication, slander and wine is of one kind. Qatada, Ibn al-Musayyib and others said: the forbidden pity is in lightening the flogging for fornication. In their view, the flogging for wine and slander is lightened and the flogging for fornication is intensified. Sulayman ibn Yasar said: pity is forbidden in both cases. Abu Mijlaz said: we stone the one subject to the punishment, but we do not drop the punishment; the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the whip, "less than this," is a form of pity. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: strike, and do not show your armpit. The people agreed that the striking is a lash between two lashes. Al-Zuhri said: the flogging for fornication and slander is severe, because they are of one meaning, and the flogging for wine is lighter.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿in the religion of God﴾ mean: in neglecting the religion of God, that is, His law. It is possible that "religion" here means "judgement."

Then He established them in the sense of firmness and urging by His words: ﴿if you believe in God﴾. This is like when you say to a man you are urging: "If you are a man, do such-and-such," meaning: these are the deeds of men.

(p-335) His words, exalted is He, ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾: the purpose of the verse is severity towards the fornicators and rebuke in the presence of people. There is no dispute that the more numerous the group, the more fitting it is for compliance with the command. People differed over the least number that suffices. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: there must be the presence of ten, and he said: this number is a collective unit beyond the single units, and it is the least of the plural. Ibn Zayd and others said: there must be the presence of four, and they held that testimony for fornication is likewise, and that this is a category of it. Al-Zuhri said: the group is three or more. 'Ata' and 'Ikrima said: there must be two at least, and this is the well-known view of Malik, who regarded it as a place of testimony. Mujahid said: one suffices and is called a group; Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, also said this. They drew evidence from His words, exalted is He: ﴿Why did not a party from every group among them go forth, that they might gain understanding in the religion?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122], and His words: ﴿And if two groups﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], which was revealed concerning the fighting of two men.

Scholars differed over banishment (taghrib). The Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may God be pleased with him, banished a man to Fadak. This is the view of 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Abu Dhar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with them all. But 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, after banishing a man who then joined the Byzantines, said: "I will not banish anyone after him." On this there are two opinions from Malik. He did not regard the banishment of women and slaves as valid, and he argued with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A woman should not travel a day's journey except with a mahram." Among those who rejected banishment altogether are the people of opinion. Al-Shafi'i said: the unmarried man is banished, whether a man or a woman. 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, banished a woman to Basra.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 3:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or an idolater; and that is forbidden to the believers.﴾

In this verse there are four aspects of interpretation.

The first is that the purpose of the verse is to denounce and shame his affair, and that it is forbidden to the believers. The connection of this meaning with what precedes it is good and eloquent. By His saying, glorified is He, "does not marry" (lā yankiḥu), he means "does not have intercourse with" (lā yaṭa'u), so that nikāḥ (marriage) carries the meaning of jimā' (sexual intercourse). He repeated the account, for emphasis, and took it from both sides. Then he added the division of the idolater (male) and the idolatress (female) in terms of shirk, which is more general among sins than zina. The meaning is: the fornicator, at the time of his fornication, has intercourse only with a fornicatress from among the Muslims, or with one who is baser than her from among the idolatresses. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his companions, that nikāḥ in this verse means waṭ' (sexual intercourse). Al-Zajjaj denied this and said: nikāḥ in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is known only in the sense of tazwīj (marrying).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not as he said, for in the Qur'an there is ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], and the Prophet ﷺ explained that it means waṭ'. Al-Tabari mentioned what tends toward this interpretation from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah, but it is not clear-cut nor complete.

The second is that the verse was revealed concerning specific people. This is an opinion whose meaning has been related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and from Ibn 'Abbas and his companions, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. They said: they were people who used to commit zina in the Jahiliyya with famous prostitutes. When Islam came and they embraced it, they could no longer commit zina, so they wished, out of poverty, to marry those women, since it was their custom to spend on those who had engaged themselves to marry them. So the verse was revealed on account of them. The indication of "the fornicator" refers to one of those men, and the name of zina that was in the Jahiliyya was applied to him. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿does not marry﴾ means does not take a wife. In the verse, according to this interpretation, there is the sense of lamenting over them, and in that there is rebuke, as if He were saying: what a calamity! The fornicator does not wish to marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, meaning their souls incline toward these base things because of their lack of self-restraint. The consensus that a fornicatress may not be married by an idolater refutes this interpretation. Then His saying: (p-337) ﴿and that is forbidden to the believers﴾, meaning the marriage of those prostitutes, so the people of this interpretation claim that Allah the Exalted forbade the marriage of those prostitutes to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Among the most famous of them was 'Anaq the prostitute, and the one who intended to marry her was DulduI, who used to smuggle the weak among the Muslims out of Makkah in secret. She became aware of him and invited him to herself, but he refused fornication and wished to marry her, and he asked the permission of the Prophet ﷺ, and the verse was revealed. When she invited him and he refused, she said to him: "How will you emerge? By Allah, I will expose you!"

Al-Tabari mentioned that among the aforementioned prostitutes were Umm Mahzul, the slave-girl of al-Sa'ib al-Makhzumi, and it is said of her: Umm Mahzum; and Umm Ghalig, the slave-girl of Safwan ibn Umayya; and Hannah the Copt, the slave-girl of al-'As ibn Wa'il; and Muznah, the slave-girl of Malik ibn 'Amilah ibn Sabbaq ibn 'Abd al-Dar; and Jallalah, the slave-girl of Suhayl ibn 'Amr; and Umm Suwayd, the slave-girl of 'Amr ibn 'Uthman al-Makhzumi; and Shurayfah, the slave-girl of Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad; and Farasah, the slave-girl of Hisham ibn Rabi'ah; and Qurayba, the slave-girl of Hilal ibn Anas; and others of them who had banners by which their dwellings were known. Likewise, in Madinah there were well-known slave-women of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and others.

Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said in the context of this interpretation: In the Jahiliyya there were houses called al-mawakhir, in which they would hire out their young women, and they were known for fornication; so Allah forbade that to the believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that this statement belongs to the interpretation I mentioned before this one. The singular of al-mawakhir is makhur (brothel), and from it is the saying of some of the later poets:

"In every valley we descended into, a dasakrah (tavern);
on every height we ascended, a makhur."

The third interpretation was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others, from al-Hasan, and it is that he said: the intended meaning is the fornicator who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment (al-mahdud) and the fornicatress who has been subjected to it. He said: this is a ruling from Allah, the Exalted, so it is not permissible for a fornicator who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment to marry anyone but one who has been subjected to it. It was narrated that a man who had been subjected to the punishment married a woman who had not been, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib annulled their marriage. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that is forbidden to the believers﴾ means zina. Al-Zahrawi related in this regard a hadith through the route of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The fornicator who has been flogged may not marry anyone but his like." This hadith is not authentic, and this opinion is open to question, and the inclusion of "the idolater" in the verse refutes it, and the wording of the verse rejects it; and even if "the idolatress" is understood to mean the kitabiyyah (women of the People of the Book), there is no way to get around the word "idolater."

The fourth has been related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and it is that he said: this ruling applied to fornicators in general, that a fornicator may not marry anyone but a fornicatress. Then the concession came and this was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And marry the single persons among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32]. The sequence of this abrogation (naskh) has also been related from Mujahid, except that he said: the prohibition was specific to those particular men, not to fornicators in general. Abu 'Ubayda mentioned this from them in his book on abrogation (al-Nasikh), and he related from Mujahid that he said: the marriage of those prostitutes was forbidden to those particular men.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The mention of "shirk" (association) in the verse weakens these approaches.

Abu al-Burhashim recited: "wa-ḥarrama Allāhu dhālika 'alā al-mu'minīn" (and Allah has forbidden that to the believers).

It has been disputed concerning one who commits zina with a woman and then wishes to marry her. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Tawus, Ibn al-Musayyab, Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ata', al-Hasan, (p-339) 'Ikrimah, Ibn 'Abbas, Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i permitted that. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and 'A'isha forbade it, and said: the two remain fornicators as long as they are together.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 4–5:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. Those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning slanderers (al-qadhifin). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its occasion was what was said about 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her. It was also said: rather, it was revealed concerning slander in general, not in that particular incident. In the verse, Allah mentions the slandering of women because it is more serious, and accusing them of immorality is more hideous and more painful to souls. The slandering of men is included in the ruling of the verse by meaning and by the consensus of the Community (ijma' al-ummah) on this, similar to His explicit mention of the flesh of swine, while its fat, its cartilage and the like are included by meaning and consensus. Al-Zahrawi related that the meaning is "the chaste persons" (al-anfus al-muhsanat), so that by its wording it encompasses men and women, and what indicates this is His saying: ﴿And the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa: 24]. The majority read the ṣād in "al-muḥṣanāt" with a fatḥa, while Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. "Al-muḥṣanāt" here means the chaste (al-'afa'if), because this is what makes the flogging of the slanderer obligatory; and chastity (al-'iffah) is the highest meaning of ihsan. Within it is Islam, and in this incident it includes freedom. From this is the saying of Hassan:

"A chaste one, dignified..........................."

From it is His saying: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. Allah mentioned among the attributes of women those that are contrary to being accused of fornication, and so that those excluded from this are those upon whom fornication has been established and others among women who have not reached intercourse, according to the difference of opinion on that.

He expressed slander by "ramy" (throwing) because of the common usage of throwing, that it is harmful like throwing a stone or an arrow. So when the slanderer's speech is harmful, it was made "ramy". This is as one said:

"........................... ∗∗∗ and the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."

And slander and ramy have one meaning.

Allah made the requirement of four witnesses strict against the slanderer, as a mercy to His servants and a veil over them. Most people recite "bi-arba'ati shuhada'" with the number construed as idafa (genitive construction) to "shuhada'". 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar and Abu Zar'ah ibn Jarir read "bi-arba'atin" with tanwin, and "shuhada'" in this reading is either a badal (substitute), or a sifah (adjective) of "arba'a", or a hal (circumstantial accusative), or a tamyiz (specification). There is scrutiny in these last two, since a hal from an indefinite noun is problematic and the tamyiz is plural, and Sibawayh holds that tanwin on the number and leaving it unconstructed is permissible only in poetry. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) regarded this reading as good and preferred it over the reading of the majority.

The ruling on the testimony of the four is that it must be based on direct observation, like the kohl-rod in the kohl-pot, in a single place. If one of them wavers, the three and the accuser are flogged, as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did in the matter of al-Mughira ibn Shu'bah. That was because Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith and his brother Nafi' — al-Zahrawi said: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith — and Ziyad, their brother through the mother — and he was attributed to Mu'awiyah — and Shibl ibn Ma'bad al-Jabali testified against him for fornication. When they came to give their testimony, Ziyad hesitated and did not give it completely, so 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, flogged the three mentioned.

Al-jald means striking; al-mujaladah means fighting with (or using) hides; then "al-jald" was borrowed for other things such as a sword and others. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"I strike them on the day of al-Hadiqah bare-handed, as if my hands with the sword were a player's whip."

"Thamanin" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and "jaldah" is in the accusative as a specification. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded that we never accept the testimony of the slanderers who have been punished, ever; and this implies for the duration of their lives. Then He judged them to be defiantly disobedient, that is, outside of obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic.

Then Allah, majestic and mighty, made an exception for those who repent and reform after the slander, for He promised them mercy and forgiveness. The verse therefore contains three rulings concerning the slanderer: flogging him, rejecting his testimony forever, and his being defiantly disobedient. The exception does not operate on his flogging, by consensus; and it operates on his disobedience, by consensus. People differed over its operation on the rejection of testimony. Shurayh the judge, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, al-Thawri, and Abu Hanifah said: the exception does not operate on the rejection of his testimony; rather only his disobedience before Allah is removed, while the testimony of a slanderer is never accepted at all, even if he repents and retracts his statement, and in no state whatsoever. The majority of people said: the exception operates on the rejection of testimony, so when the slanderer repents his testimony is accepted. Then they differed over the form of his repentance. The position of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Sha'bi and others, is that his repentance is only by his retracting himself regarding that slander for which he was punished, and so did Shibl ibn Ma'bad and Nafi', who repented of the accusation against al-Mughira and retracted themselves, so 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, accepted their testimony; but Abu Bakrah Nufay' refused to retract, so 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, rejected his testimony until he died. A group, among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others, said: his repentance is that he reforms and his condition becomes good, even if he does not retract his statement by denial.

The jurists of the Malikis differed as to when the testimony of the slanderer falls. Ibn al-Majishun said: by the very act of slander. Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab, and Sahnun said: it does not fall until he is flogged; and if something prevents his flogging (a pardon or otherwise), his testimony is not rejected. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: his testimony during the period of the term regarding establishing (a claim) is suspended, and he preferred the view that repentance is either by denial of the slander, or otherwise what return is there for a just person who slandered, was flogged, and remained upon his uprightness? "Tabu" means: they returned.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a preference, and al-Tabari and others preferred the view of Malik.

Also differing, on the view that his testimony is permissible after repentance, as to what kind of testimony is permissible: Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is permissible in everything without restriction, and likewise everyone who has been flogged for anything. Sahnun, may Allah have mercy on him, said: whoever has been flogged for any matter, his testimony is not permissible regarding the like of what he was flogged for. Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: whoever has been flogged for slander or fornication, his testimony is not permissible in any aspect of fornication, nor in slander, nor in li'an, even if he is just. They related this view from Malik. And they agreed, as far as I know, concerning the child of fornication, that his testimony is not permissible in matters of fornication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 6–10:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah, that he is surely of the truthful.﴾ ﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But it will avert the punishment from her if she testifies four testimonies by Allah that he is surely of the liars.﴾ ﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he is of the truthful.﴾ ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Accepting of repentance, Wise...﴾

When the preceding verse was revealed concerning those who accuse chaste women, its apparent meaning encompassed husbands and others. Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I find a man with my wife, shall I give him time until I bring four witnesses? By Allah, I will strike him with the sword, without turning away from him." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you marvel at the jealousy of Sa'd? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me." There are various narrations of Sa'd's words, (p-344) approximating this meaning. Then after that came Hilal ibn Umayya al-Waqifi, who accused his wife with Shurayk ibn al-Sahma' al-Balawi, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ resolved to strike him with the hadd for slander, and then this verse was revealed. At that point the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered the two of them in the mosque, and they performed mutual cursing (li'an). The woman hesitated at the fifth [oath] when she was admonished and it was said that she was liable [to punishment], so she said: "I will not disgrace my people for the rest of the day," and persisted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ separated them, and she gave birth to a boy who resembled a dark-grey camel; afterwards that boy became a governor in Egypt, while not knowing a father for himself. Also came 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, who accused his wife and performed li'an. It is well known that the incident of Hilal was earlier and was the cause of the verse; it was said that the incident of 'Uwaymir was earlier, and he is the one who brought 'Asim ibn 'Adi to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as an intermediary.

The word "al-azwaj" (the wives) in this ruling includes Muslim women, non-Muslim women, and slave women; the husband performs li'an with all of them to disown the child from pregnancy, while the free woman is specifically entitled to ward off the hadd for slander from herself.

(p-345) Al-Jumhur read "arba'a shahadat" in the accusative, as the accusative of a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element is His saying "fa-shahadatu" (then the testimony). The nominative "shahadatu" is read as the predicate of an inchoative, with the implied sense: "then the ruling is" or "then the obligatory [matter] is," or as an inchoative with the implied sense "then it is incumbent upon them to testify," or with the predicate omitted and understood at the end of the verse as: "sufficient" or "obligatory."

His saying, the Exalted, "bi-Allah" is related to "shahadat," and it is permissible that it be related to "fa-shahadatu."

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "arba'u shahadat" in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of His saying "fa-shahadatu." Abu Hatim said: there is no justification for the nominative, because the testimony is not four testimonies, and "bi-Allah," on this reading, is related to "shahadat," and it is not permissible for it to be related to "fa-shahadatu," because you would be separating the relative clause from the relative by the predicate, which is "arba'a shahadat."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿innahu la-mina al-sadiqin﴾ — according to the one who read ﴿arba'a shahadat﴾ in the accusative, it may be related to "shahadatu," and it is a clause in a position of accusative, because "the testimony" has made it occupy the position of the object. According to the one who read ﴿arba'u shahadat﴾ in the nominative, His saying ﴿innahu la-mina al-sadiqin﴾ is related to "shahadat" for the reason of the separation mentioned earlier in His saying "bi-Allah."

Hafs from 'Asim read "wal-khamisata" in the accusative in the second place, and Talhah ibn Musarrif, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, and al-A'mash read it in the accusative in both places. Al-Jumhur read "wal-khamisatu" in the nominative in both places. As for the one who read it in the accusative: if his reading of His saying "arba'a shuhadat" was in the accusative, then he conjoins "al-khamisata" to that, because it is one of the testimonies; and if he reads "arba'u shahadat" in the nominative, then he takes the accusative of "wal-khamisata" as governed by a verb implied by the preceding speech, its estimate being: "and she testifies the fifth." As for the one who read "wal-khamisatu" in the nominative: if he reads "arba'u shahadat" in the nominative, then "wal-khamisatu" is conjoined to that; and if he reads "arba'a shahadat" in the accusative, then he treats "wal-khamisata" according to the sense, because the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-shahadatu ahadihim arba'u shahadat﴾ is: "upon them are four testimonies and the fifth." Abu 'Ali cited for this the poet's usage:

"And a cracked one, as for his equal..... the verse......"

(p-346) according to his saying:

"..................... ∗∗∗ except the stationary embers of their fire, which are dust"

because the meaning is: "then stationary embers." There is no disagreement among the Seven regarding the nominative of His saying, the Exalted, "wal-khamisatu" in the first place; the disagreement among the Seven is only in the second place. Its accusative is governed by His saying ﴿an tashhada arba'a﴾, and "wal-khamisata" is by way of cutting off (qat') and taking according to the sense.

(p-347) Nafi' read "an la'nata Allah" and "an ghadiba Allah." Al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja', and 'Isa read "an la'natu Allah" and "an ghadaba Allah." This is on the supposition of the omitted subject (idmar al-amr), and it is the light (mukhaffafah) form, as it is in the saying of the poet:

"Among youths like the swords of India, they have known that every one who goes barefoot and sandal-wearing is doomed."

The remaining Seven read "anna la'nata Allah" and "anna ghadaba Allah" with the nun doubled in both and the lam'ana and ghadab in the accusative. Al-Akhfash preferred the reading with the doubled nun, because the light form is intended only for the heavy form, and the subject and matter are implied with it; whatever does not require an implied element with it is preferable.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Especially since the light form, according to Nafi's reading in His saying "an ghadaba Allah," is directly followed by the verb (p-348). Abu 'Ali said: The people of Arabic grammar find it objectionable that a verb should directly follow it, unless a separator comes between it and the verb, such as His saying ﴿'alima an sayakunu﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His saying ﴿afala yaraw alla yarji'u ilayhim qawla﴾ [Ta-Ha: 89]. As for His saying ﴿wa-an laysa lil-insani illa ma sa'a﴾ [al-Najm: 39], that is due to the weak firmness of "laysa" among verbs. As for His saying ﴿an buriku man fi al-nar﴾ [al-Naml: 8], "burika" is in the sense of supplication, so the separator was not permitted, lest it corrupt the meaning.

The "punishment averted" (al-'adhab al-mudra') in the words of the scholars is the hadd; al-Tabari related from others that it is imprisonment, and this is the view of the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), who say that there is no hadd upon her if she does not perform li'an, and the husband's statement does not make it obligatory upon her.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the hadith is that she paused at the fifth when she hesitated, then she proceeded in her li'an, and that she was to be punished with the hadd, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to her: "The punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter."

The curse was made for the lying man because he is a fabricator and a deceiver by speech, so he is removed by the curse; and the wrath, which is more severe, was made for the woman who committed the sin in deed, then lied and deceived by speech. This is the meaning of these words, and Allah knows best.

It is necessary that we mention, in the explanation of this verse, the issues related to li'an that cannot be dispensed with in knowing its ruling and when it is obligatory. Malik and his companions agreed on the obligation of li'an upon claiming to have seen zina with no intercourse by the husband, and likewise is the well-known school position; and Malik's view that li'an is obligatory upon denying a pregnancy claimed before it, with istibra' (waiting period). Al-Lakhmi related from Muhammad ibn Abi Safra that he said: li'an does not dissolve the marriage bond, based on the saying of 'Uwaymir: "I have lied about her, O Messenger of Allah, if I keep her," and he said: "Then he divorces her." The well-known school position is that the completion of li'an between them is itself a separation, and no judge's separation is needed with it. Ibn Abi Safra is not a figure whose view is set against the majority. The school of al-Shafi'i holds that separation occurs immediately upon the husband's li'an alone; Abu Hanifah and his companions said: there is no separation except by the ruling of the authority after the completion of both their li'ans; if one of them dies after the completion of both li'ans and before the judge's ruling, the other inherits from him. The school of the Mudawwana holds that the ruling of li'an separation is the ruling of divorce, and the full dowry is given to a woman not yet consummated with; in the Mukhtasar of Ibn al-Jallab: she has nothing; and this is based on the view that separation by li'an is a annulment (faskh). Ibn al-Qassar said: separation by li'an is, according to us, an annulment.

The prohibition by li'an is permanent by consensus, as far as I know, in the school of Malik, Allah have mercy on him; and some jurists of Kufa and others do not consider it permanent. If he retracts his accusation after li'an, it does not benefit him. It is related from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah that if he retracts after li'an, he becomes one of the ordinary suitors. If the woman goes first in li'an, Ibn al-Qasim said: she does not repeat it; Ashhab said: she repeats it.

The answer in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy...﴾ the verse, is omitted, its estimate being: (p-351) "He would have exposed the fornicators with something easier than this, or He would have seized them with punishment from Him, or something like this of the meanings which the omission of the answer necessitates estimating."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, those who came up with the slander are a faction among you. Do not consider it bad for you; rather, it is good for you. For every person among them is what he earned of the sin, and the one among them who took upon himself its greater part will have a great punishment.﴾

This verse and what follows it, up to sixteen verses, were revealed concerning 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, and what was connected with the matter of the slander (al-ifk). In al-Bukhari, in the account of the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, it is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "Allah revealed the ten verses, and then Allah revealed this concerning my innocence."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So it seems she counted what was specific to her.

And "al-ifk" means falsehood and lying, and "afakk" means a great liar. "Al-ifk" is turning a reality away from its state through statements and diverting it from the direction of rightness, and for this reason lying is likened to it.

The summary of the hadith of "the slander" is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out with 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, accompanying him on the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, which is the expedition of al-Muraysi'. Ibn Ishaq said: it was in the year six. Musa ibn 'Uqba said: it was in the year four. A necklace of hers was lost there. When she returned to the camel-litter (rahl) she became aware of its loss, so she went back searching for it, and the people set off at that time. She found it and returned, but she found no one. She was a young woman, thin of flesh, and the men lifted her howdah without noticing its removal. When she found no one, she lay down in her place, hoping that she would be missed and that they would come back for her. She fell asleep in that place, and nothing woke her except the saying of Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return." That was because he had lagged behind the army to guard the rearguard (al-saqa); it was also said that it was by chance. When he passed by her figure he drew near and recognized her, so he said the istirja' and said: "The wife of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was left behind here?" He dismounted from his camel and withdrew from her until 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, mounted, and he began leading her until he brought her to the army at the height of midday. Then the People of the Slander fell into their talk. The one around whom it gathered, who took it up, spread it, and kindled it was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the hypocrite. Among those who joined in his talk were Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthatha, and Hamna bint Jahsh. This is the summary of the hadith; its full and perfected form is in al-Bukhari and Muslim, and it is more complete in Muslim.

Safwan was the companion of the rearguard of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his campaigns, for his bravery, and he was among the best of the Companions. When he heard what the people said about him, he said: "Glory be to Allah! By Allah, I never uncovered the veil of any woman ever." He meant: [by way of] fornication. This is indicated by his hadith related concerning his wife, and by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about his two sons: "They resemble him more than a crow resembles a crow." It was also said that he was a hasur, who did not approach women. Ibn Ishaq mentioned this through the chain of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. He was killed as a martyr, may Allah be pleased with him, in the expedition of Armenia in the year nineteen in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also said: in the lands of the Romans in the year fifty-eight in the time of Mu'awiya.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "a faction" ('usba) is in the nominative as an apposition (badal) to the pronoun in "came" (jaa'u), and the predicate of "inna" is in His saying, glorified is He: "do not consider it" (la tahsabuhu). The estimate is: "Indeed the act of those who..." This is more coherent in meaning and more beneficial than that "a faction" should be the predicate. "Al-'usba" is a group from ten up to forty, as stated by Ya'qub and others; "'usba" is not said of fewer than ten. Of the People of the Slander, only Hassan, Mistah, Hamna, and 'Abdullah were named, and the others remained unknown; this was said by 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr when 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan asked him about this, and he said: "Indeed they were a faction, as Allah Exalted has said."

His saying, Exalted is He: "do not consider it" is addressed to everyone among the believers whom it grieved. His saying: ﴿rather, it is good for you﴾ means that it is an absolution in this world, and an elevation from Allah, blessed and exalted, in that His revelation came down with the innocence from it, and a great reward in the Hereafter, and an admonition to the believers throughout future time, and a retribution upon the slanderers in this world and the Hereafter. Therefore in that is healing and good. These are five aspects. His saying: "among them" refers back to the mentioned faction. "Iktasaba" (earned) is used for sins and the like because it indicates effort and intention, so it is more emphatic in arrangement; "kasaba" is used for good, because its attainment makes unnecessary any indication of effort in it. "Kasaba" may be used for both aspects, and similar to it is the verse:

"...and you carried Barra, and you bore Fajar."

And the indication in His saying: ﴿and the one who took upon himself its greater part﴾ is to 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the punishment threatened with it is the punishment of the Hereafter. This is the saying of the majority and is the apparent meaning of the hadith. It is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that Hassan ibn Thabit came to her one day, and he had gone blind, and he recited his praise of her:

"Chaste, grave, who is not suspected of doubt, and who in the morning is hungry for the flesh of the heedless."

'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said to him: "But you are not like that," meaning that he had fallen into [speaking of] the heedless. Then he recited:

"If what has been said of me is what I said, may my fingers never lift my whip to me."

When he left, Masruq said to her: "Does this man enter upon you, when he has said what he said, and Allah has threatened him with punishment for taking upon himself the greater part of the slander?" 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "What punishment is more severe than blindness and the striking of the hadd?" In another narration: "and a blow with the sword?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for her saying about the hadd, Hassan, Mistah, and Hamna were given the hadd. Ibn Ishaq mentioned this, and al-Tirmidhi mentioned it. In the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is stated that Ibn Ubayy was given the hadd, but this, in my view, is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, because it is not preserved that 'Abdullah was accused. 'Urwa said in al-Bukhari: "I was informed that he used to have it spread and talked about in his presence, and he would approve of it, listen to it, and spread it."

As for the blow with the sword: when Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal heard Hassan's saying about the slander, he came and struck him with the sword on his head, and said:

"Meet the edge of the sword on my behalf, for I am a youth who, when provoked, is not a poet."

A group seized Safwan, bound him by the collar, and brought him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then waived the wound of Hassan and asked that it be given to him. This implies that Hassan was among those who took upon himself the greater part.

Some have said: the indication by "the one who" is to the initiator of this calumny and the one who fabricated it. So for each of them is what he earned, and for the initiating fabricator is a great punishment. On this view, he is unspecified. This is the saying of al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. Abu Zayd and others said: it is 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy.

Most of the people read "kibrahu" with a kasra on the kaf. Hamid al-A'raj, Ya'qub al-Zuhri, Abu Raja', al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "kubrahu" with a damma on the kaf. Both are verbal nouns (masdar) from "kibr al-shay'" (the greatness and magnitude of a thing). But the Arabs used the damma on the kaf for age: one says "hadha kubr al-qawm," meaning the eldest of the people in age and standing. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the story of Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa: "The eldest (al-kubr)." From its use in the second meaning is the saying of Ibn al-Hatim:

"She sleeps through the greatness of her affair, and when she rises slowly, she nearly stumbles."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 12–13:

His Exalted and Majestic Words:

﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own kind and say, "This is a manifest lie"?﴾ ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses to it? Since they did not bring the witnesses, those—with Allah—are the liars.﴾

The address in these two verses is to all the believers, except for those who took upon themselves the great part of it (al-Kibr). It is possible that they are included in the address too, and in this there is a rebuke to the believers, meaning: denouncing it was obligatory upon them. The meaning is that the distinguished believing men and women should have measured the matter against themselves; so if that was far-fetched regarding themselves, they should have judged that it was even further-fetched regarding Safwan and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, because of their merit. It is related that this sound reasoning came from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and his wife, when "he entered upon her and she said to him: 'O Abu Ayyub, have you heard what has been said?' He said: 'Yes, and that is a lie. Would you, O Umm Ayyub, do such a thing?' She said: 'No, by Allah.' He said: 'By Allah, 'A'isha is better than you.' Umm Ayyub said: 'Yes.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That act and its like is what Allah rebuked the believers for, since not all of them did it. The pronoun in His words "jaa'u" (they brought) refers to those who took upon themselves the great part of it. And since they are liars in the sight of Allah, the reality applies to them, and at this point the legal punishment (hadd) was imposed on them. It is not reported in the well-known collections that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was given the hadd, and it seems that this was not done because no clear evidence (bayyina) was established against him for the statement, due to his hypocrisy and concealment; he was only immersing himself in it with those who spread it, and he did not seek the testimony for it, as 'Urwa said in al-Bukhari: "I was informed that he used to confirm it and seek it out."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

But the Prophet (ﷺ) asked to be excused from him on the pulpit, and rebuked him with words, and there occurred regarding his affair between the Aws and the Khazraj what is lengthy in Muslim, within the whole of the hadith of the Slander (al-Ifk).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 14–18:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into.﴾ ﴿When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of, and you thought it trivial while it was, with Allah, tremendous.﴾ ﴿And why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a great slander"?﴾ ﴿Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it, if you are believers.﴾ ﴿And Allah makes clear to you the verses, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

This is a forceful reproach from Allah, the Exalted. He mentions that their state, in which all of them fell, was one of passing on the talk and taking it up, even though neither the one who reported it nor the one it was reported about was a confirmed (true) party; rather, the very act of passing it on and receiving it from tongue to tongue, and plunging deeply into the talk, is what the reproach is directed at.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "إذْ تُلْقُونَهُ" (idh tulqūnahu) with a damma on the taa', a sukun on the lam, and a damma on the qaf, from al-IlqĀ' (casting/throwing); this is a clear reading. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud recited "إذْ تَتَلَقَّوْنَهُ" (idh tatalaqqawnahu) from al-talaqqi (receiving) with two taa's. The majority of the Seven recited "إذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ" (idh talaqqawnahu) with one taa' dropped and the dhal made manifest without idgham (assimilation); this too is from al-talaqqi. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited "إذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ" with idgham of the dhal into the taa'. Ibn Kathir recited "إذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ" with the dhal made manifest and the taa' assimilated into the taa', and this reading is problematic because it requires the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters; it is not like the idgham in the reading of those who recited "فَلا تَناجَوْا" and "وَلا تَنابَزُوا", because the softness of the quiescent alif and its being a letter of extension made that acceptable there, which is not acceptable with the sukun of the dhal. Ibn Ya'mur and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her—and she is the most knowledgeable of people in this matter—recited "إذْ تَلِقُونَهُ" with a fatha on the taa', a kasra on the lam, and a damma on the qaf. The meaning of this reading comes from the Arabic saying "وَلِقَ الرَجُلُ ولَقًا" (walaqa al-rajulu walaqan), meaning he lied. Ibn Sidah said in "al-Muhkam": it was read "إذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ", and the lexicographers relate that it is from walaqa, meaning he lied; they brought the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive one. In my view, he intended: "إذْ تُلْقُونَ فِيهِ" (idh tulquna fihi), so he dropped the preposition and attached the pronoun directly. Al-Tabari and others relate that this word is derived from al-walq, which is your rushing at a thing after another thing, like an enemy following an enemy, and speech following speech. It is said: walaqa in his course, if he hastened. From this is the poet's saying:

"She brought him, a she-camel from Syria, swift in pace."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you say with your mouths﴾ is intensification, insistence and emphasis. The pronoun in His saying "وَتَحْسَبُونَهُ" (and you reckon it) refers to the talk, the plunging into it, and its spreading. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And why, when you heard it﴾ down to ﴿and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a reproach addressed to all the believers, meaning: it was incumbent upon you to disapprove of it, and that none of you should take it up from another by way of relating and transmitting; and that you should declare Allah exalted above such a thing occurring from the wife of His Prophet ﷺ; and that you should judge this statement to be a slander. The reality of slander (buhtan) is that something is said of a person that is not in him, whereas backbiting (ghiba) is that something is said of a person that is in him. Then Allah admonished them against returning to such a state, and "أنْ" (an) is an object of purpose, with the implied meaning "out of aversion to" or similar. His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾ is a warning and emphasis, as you would say: "It is fitting for you to do such and such if you are a man." The rest of the verse is clear, and "عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ" (All-Knowing, All-Wise) are two attributes that the verse requires.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 19–20:

(p-360) His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, those who love that immorality should be spread among those who have believed will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾ ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Kind and Merciful...﴾

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the reference of this verse is to the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those like him, and it is specific to the matter of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Their love for the spreading of immorality among the believers is firmly established in its literal sense, because of their enmity toward the people of faith. Their painful punishment in this world is the prescribed penalties (hudud), and in the Hereafter, the Fire.

A group said, and their view is the more apparent: the verse is general, covering every slanderer, whether he is a hypocrite or a believer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The believing slanderer does not possess a love for the spread of immorality among the believers in its entirety, but he loves it for his victim; likewise another for his victim, and another, until immorality spreads from the totality of their actions. Thus they are lovers of it in this respect, insofar as each one loves a part of its spread. The painful punishment in this world is the prescribed penalties, and in the Hereafter it admits of two aspects. The first is that the slanderer is threatened, among the sinners, with a punishment in the Hereafter that the prescribed penalty does not remove, according to the requirement of the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, and his case is like the case of those who wage war and are crucified: disgrace in this world and for them in the Hereafter a punishment. The second aspect is that it is judged that the prescribed penalty removes the punishment of the Hereafter according to the hadith of 'Ubada, and that His statement "and the Hereafter" (p-361) does not intend the generality of slanderers, but intends either the hypocrites or those who did not repent. Al-Tabari said: its meaning is: if he dies persisting, not repentant.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows﴾ means: the innocent one from the guilty one, and all other matters, and the wisdom in concealing you and in the severity of the warning and punishment upon your slanderers.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah﴾ the verse... The answer to "lawla" is omitted, being indicated by the context. Its estimate: He would have exposed you for your sins and not concealed you, and would have punished you for what you plunged into of false speech and slander.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 21:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan. And whoever follows the steps of Satan - indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing. And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would have ever been purified, but Allah purifies whom He wills. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

This address is general to all the believers. "Khutuwat" (steps) is the plural of "khutwa," which is the distance between the two feet in walking. So the meaning is: do not walk in His paths and roads of evil deeds. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is possible that "khutuwat" is the plural of "khata'" (error) from the wrongdoing, and the hamza was eased so that it was pronounced "khutuwat." The majority (al-Jumhur) read the "ta'" of "khutuwat" with a damma, while 'Asim and al-A'mash read it with a sukun.

The majority read "ma zaka" with a light kaf, meaning: he did not become guided, nor did he submit, nor did he recognize right guidance. Abu Haywa, al-Hasan, and al-A'mash read "ma zakka" with a shadda on the kaf, meaning: their purification, their cleansing, and their guidance are only by His bounty, not by your deeds and your guarding yourselves from sins. Then the Exalted mentioned that He purifies whom He wills, from among those for whom happiness had preceded, and whose righteous deed was a sign of the prior decree of happiness for them.

Then the Exalted informed that He is Hearing of all their sayings and speech, including slander and other things, and Knowing of the truth of that from its falsehood. It is not permissible for Him, in that regard, to have doubt or error.

(p-362)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to the near of kin, the needy, and those who emigrated in the way of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

The well-known report is that this verse was revealed concerning the affair of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, son of Abu Quhafa, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mistah ibn Uthatha. The reason was that Mistah was the son of his maternal aunt, and he was among the emigrants, the Badri participants, and the needy. Mistah ibn Uthatha ibn 'Abbad ibn al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is said that his name was 'Awf, and Mistah is a nickname. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to spend on him because of his poverty. When the affair of the slander occurred and Mistah said what he said, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, swore that he would not spend on him and would never benefit him with any benefit. Mistah came and apologized, saying: "I only used to frequent the gathering of Hassan and would listen without speaking." Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "You have laughed and shared in what was said." And he passed by his right side, and the verse was revealed.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: A group of the believers cut off their benefits from everyone who had spoken in the slander and said: "By Allah, we will not join ties with anyone who spoke about the matter of 'A'isha." So the verse was revealed concerning all of them. The first view is more sound, but the verse encompasses the Community until the Day of Resurrection, that a person of virtue and wealth should not become enraged and swear never to benefit whoever has this attribute for the remainder of time.

The jurists held that whoever swears not to do a Sunna (recommended practice) of the Sunnas or a recommended act, and makes that perpetual, his testimony is thereby impaired. Al-Balkhi mentioned this in al-Muntaqa. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Where is the one who swears against Allah that he will not do good?"

"Ya'tali" means: he swears. Its form is yaf'ali, from al-alya (al-ilya), which is the oath. A group said: its meaning is: he falls short, from your saying: "alawtu fi kadha" when you fell short in it, and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they spare no effort to corrupt you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited: "wa la yatalla," and this form is yatafa''al from al-alya without disagreement. In the Mushaf it is written as "ya, ta, lam," and therefore this variant was permissible for Abu Ja'far and Zayd, and they transmitted it. Al-Tabari mentioned that the script of the Mushaf agrees with the recitation of the majority, and the apparent sense of his statement is that there is an alif before the ta'.

"Al-fadl wa al-si'a" here means: wealth. His saying, exalted is He: "Do you not love..." is an illustration and an argument, i.e., just as you love Allah's forgiveness of your sins, so too should you forgive those below you. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy," relates to this meaning. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed I love that Allah forgive me," and he restored to Mistah the maintenance and the kindness that had been flowing to him. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "And he atoned for his oath." Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and Sufyan ibn Husayn recited: "wa paltaʿfu wa paltasfahu" with the ta' from above in both, and this was related from the Prophet ﷺ.

Some people said: this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in terms of the gentleness of Allah toward the slanderers who are sinners through this wording.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse only gives a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this world, while hope lies in the Hereafter. As for hope in this verse being by analogy, i.e., when He commands those of wealth to pardon, this bounty is extended by the breadth of His mercy, there is no lord other than Him. The verses of hope are His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and His saying: ﴿Allah is Gentle with His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19]. I heard my father, may Allah have mercy on him, say: the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, in my view, is His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47]. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has said in another verse: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, in gardens of paradise, for them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 22]. So He explained the great bounty in this verse and gave good tidings of it to the believers in that one. Some of them said: the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is His saying: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5], because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not be content with the remaining of anyone from his Community in the Fire.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 24, verses 23–25:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and theirs will be a great punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense, and they will know that Allah is the Truth, the Manifest.﴾

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: This verse, which contains the curse upon the slanderer and a severe warning to him, refers specifically to those who slandered ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, al-Ḍaḥḥak, and others said: Rather, it applies to all the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah made the matter of slandering them grave because of their station in the religion, so He cursed whoever slanders them and did not attach repentance to the end of the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The slanderer of other than them bears the name of *fisq* (grave sin), and repentance is mentioned for him.

A group of scholars said: Rather, it concerns the matter of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, but it is meant to include everyone who possesses this attribute. Some of this group said: This verse was first revealed concerning the slanderers, and after that the verse in the surah that contains repentance was revealed. The discussion of "*al-muḥṣanāt*" (the chaste women) has already been given earlier, with a similar meaning.

The word "*al-laʿna*" (the curse) in this verse means: distance (from Allah's mercy), the imposition of the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*), the believers' sense of aversion from them, their shunning by the believers, and their loss of the rank of *ʿadala* (moral uprightness, i.e., acceptability as a witness). According to the one who says this verse is specifically about ʿĀʾisha, these severe consequences apply to ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy and those like him. Included within the slandering of a chaste woman is the slandering of the man with her, and he may be a believer.

The governing element of the word "*yawma*" (on the day) in His words is an implied verb required by "*al-ʿadhāb*" (the punishment), meaning: "they will be punished on a day," or something similar. Allah the Exalted informed us that their limbs will testify against them, and this is among the greatest of humiliations and retribution. Allah made the matter of slandering them grave because of their station in the religion, so He cursed whoever slanders them and did not attach repentance to the end of the verse.

The slanderer of other than them bears the name of *fisq* (grave sin), and repentance is mentioned for him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 26:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women.﴾ ﴿Those are declared free of what they say; for them is forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾

The interpreters (al-mutawwilun) differed concerning what is described as wicked (khabith) and good (tayyib) in this verse. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: it refers to statements and actions. Then this group differed. Some of them said: the meaning is that wicked words and wicked deeds are not uttered by anyone, nor are they approved, except by wicked people among mankind; so they belong to them and they belong to such deeds in this respect. Likewise, good things are for good people. Others among them said: the meaning is that wicked words and wicked deeds do not fit, nor do they cling, when the slanderer hurls his accusation and the accuser casts his charge, except upon wicked people among mankind; so they belong to them and they belong to such deeds in this respect.

Ibn Zayd said: what is described as wicked and good are women and men. The verse is in the manner of the one that precedes it, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. So the meaning of this one is to distinguish between the ruling concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his likes, and the ruling concerning the Prophet, ﷺ, and the excellent Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them, and his community. That is: the Prophet ﷺ is good, so Allah has not given him except every good woman; and those [others] are wicked, so they belong to the wicked women.

(p-367) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

By this verse it was said of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ that they are "the good women who are declared free."

His saying, exalted is He: "Those" refers to "the good men" in His saying: ﴿and good men are for good women﴾. al-Naqqash said: the indication by ﴿Those are declared free﴾ refers to Safwan and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he combined them in the pronoun according to the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he has brothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], while what is meant is two brothers.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this citing of the verse of siblings there is room for consideration. According to these meanings, the referent of the pronoun in "yaqulun" is determined, so reflect upon it. Then Allah, exalted is He, promised the good men among the believers forgiveness at the reckoning, and a generous provision in Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants. That is better for you; perhaps you will be reminded.﴾ ﴿And if you do not find anyone in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

The occasion of this verse, as al-Tabari mentioned from 'Udayy ibn Thabit: "A woman from the Ansar said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am in my home in a state that I do not like anyone, whether a parent or a child, to see me in, and a man from my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state.' So this verse was revealed." Then it is general for the community until the end of time, insofar as this incident applies to each person individually. A person's house is the house in which no one else is with him, or the house in which his wife and his female slave are. Whatever is other than this is other than his house. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: "It is fitting for a person not to enter the house in which his mother is except after seeking familiarity (istintas)." And it was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I ask permission to enter upon my mother?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'But she is my mother, and she has no servant other than me.' He said: 'Would you like to see her naked?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then ask permission to enter upon her.'" Likewise every woman within the prohibited degrees (dhat mahram) of him, because it is not fitting that he should see them naked. Zaynab, the wife of Ibn Mas'ud, said: "When Ibn Mas'ud came to his house, he would clear his throat, for fear that he might come upon something he disliked."

The meaning of "tasta'nisu" is: you seek to know (tasta'limu), i.e., you seek knowledge of who is in the house and look to get insight. You say "anastu" when you know by sense, and when you see. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you perceive in them maturity of judgment, then hand over to them their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and His saying: "I perceived a fire" (anastu naran). From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"Look, my friend, at the gate of Jillaq; do you perceive, beyond al-Balqa', anyone?"

And the saying of al-Harith:

"I perceived a sound... the house..."

The form of "anasa" is af'ala, and "istana'sa" is istaf'ala. So the meaning of "tasta'nisun" is: you seek what gives you and the people of the house among you familiarity. When a person wishes to know the affair of the house he intends to enter, that happens through asking permission of those within, or by clearing his throat and making his presence known in whatever way he can, pausing for as long as is needed to take precaution, and then entering after that.

Al-Tabari held that "tasta'nisu" means: until you make the people of the house familiar with you by clearing your throat, asking permission and the like, and make yourselves familiar by knowing that you have been made known. But the conjugation of the verb rejects that it derives from "anasa".

Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he used to read: "hatta tasta'dhinu wa tusallimu," and this is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Abu Hatim transmitted "hatta tusallimu wa tasta'dhinu." Ibn 'Abbas said: "tasta'nisu" is an error or a slip of the scribes.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All the codices of the Muslims have "tasta'nisu" recorded in them, and consensus was established concerning them from the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. They are the ones whose opposition is not permitted. The reading "yasta'dhinu" is weak. To attribute error and slip to the scribes in a wording upon which the Companions unanimously agreed is a statement that is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The more likely view is that "tasta'dhinu" is an explanation (of the meaning). The apparent sense of what al-Tabari transmitted is that it is a reading, but it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "tasta'nisu" means "tasta'dhinu." Among what negates this statement from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is that "tasta'nisu" is firmly established in meaning, clear in its aspect in the speech of the Arabs, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Shall I seek familiarity (asta'nisu), O Messenger of Allah?" while 'Umar was standing at the door of the upper room... the well-known hadith. That requires that he sought familiarity with him (ﷺ). So how would Ibn 'Abbas (p-370) may Allah be pleased with both of them, declare the Companions of the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, to be in error in a matter like this?

Al-Tabari also transmitted with a chain from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that they said: the first verse was abrogated, and the exception from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited﴾ [al-Nur: 29]. This too does not involve abrogation or exception, because the first verse concerns inhabited and private houses, and the second verse concerns those that are open to entry. It seems that whoever held the view of exception regarded the first as general.

The form of seeking permission is that a man says: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" If he is permitted, he enters; if he is told to go back, he departs; and if he is ignored, he asks permission three times, then departs after the three. As for the establishment of what I have mentioned of the form of asking permission, al-Tabari related that "a man came to the house of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Shall I enter? Or may I enter?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a female slave of his called Rawda: 'Say to this one: He says: Peace be upon you, may I enter?' The man heard it and said it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Enter.'" It was also related that Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was once afflicted by the scorching heat, so he came to the tent of a woman of Quraysh and said: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" The woman said: "Enter with peace." He repeated, and she repeated, so he said to her: "Say: Enter." She said that, and he entered. It seems he paused when she said "with peace," because the wording could mean: enter with your greeting, not with your person. Then every people have their customary phrasing in asking permission. As for the establishment of returning after asking permission three times, it is based on the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, whom 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, employed, and to which Abu Sa'id al-Khudri testified on behalf of Abu Musa, and then Ubayy ibn Ka'b... the well-known hadith. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: seeking permission is obligatory upon every person who has reached puberty, and the mention of this will come (p-371). Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man's messenger is his permission," meaning: when he sends someone, he has given him permission to enter. His saying: ﴿That is better for you﴾ completes the statement at that point. His saying: ﴿perhaps you will be reminded﴾ means: We did that for you and alerted you, so that perhaps you...

The pronoun in His saying: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾ refers to the houses that belong to others. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾ is: if there is no property of yours in them. Al-Tabari rejected this interpretation, and indeed it is extremely weak. It seems Mujahid regarded uninhabited houses as entered without permission only if the entrant has property in them, and he understood the word "mata'" (property) as the household goods, namely the carpets and clothes. All of this is weak.

Qatada is also reported to have said: a man from the Muhajirun said: "I sought this verse my whole life and did not attain it: that I seek permission to enter upon one of my brothers and he says to me, 'Go back,' so I go back, and I am glad at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are told, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you.﴾"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ is a warning to those who spy on houses and seek to enter while people are heedless, for the sake of sins and looking at what is not lawful, and to others who fall into what is forbidden.
