His saying: ﴿That is better for you﴾ completes the statement at that point. His saying: ﴿perhaps you will be reminded﴾ means: We did that for you and alerted you, so that perhaps you...

The pronoun in His saying: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾ refers to the houses that belong to others. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾ is: if there is no property of yours in them. Al-Tabari rejected this interpretation, and indeed it is extremely weak. It seems Mujahid regarded uninhabited houses as entered without permission only if the entrant has property in them, and he understood the word "mata'" (property) as the household goods, namely the carpets and clothes. All of this is weak.

Qatada is also reported to have said: a man from the Muhajirun said: "I sought this verse my whole life and did not attain it: that I seek permission to enter upon one of my brothers and he says to me, 'Go back,' so I go back, and I am glad at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are told, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you.﴾"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ is a warning to those who spy on houses and seek to enter while people are heedless, for the sake of sins and looking at what is not lawful, and to others who fall into what is forbidden.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses wherein is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

It is narrated that when the verse of seeking permission (al-isti'dhan) was revealed, a certain man went to excess in the matter: he would not come to any place, whether ruined or inhabited, without greeting and asking permission. So this verse was revealed, and Allah, exalted is He, permitted in it the lifting of the requirement of seeking permission for every house in which no one dwells, because the reason (al-'illa) for seeking permission is only the fear of exposure of what is sacred (al-hurumat). When the reason is removed, the ruling is removed.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) gave several examples of these houses. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Qatada and Mujahid said: they are the inns (al-fanadiq) on the roads of travellers. Mujahid said: no one dwells in them; rather they are (p-372) set aside so that every wayfarer (ibn sabil) may take shelter in them, and "wherein is provision for you" means enjoyment of their benefit. 'Ata' gave the example of uninhabited ruins (al-kharib) into which a person enters to urinate and defecate; in this too there is provision. Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: they are the shops of the markets (al-qaysariyyat) and the bazaar. Al-Sha'bi said: because they bring their goods and place them in them and say to people: "Come along." This view is held by one who erred, for the houses of the qaysariyya are protected by the property of people, not permitted to everyone who wishes to enter them by consensus (ijma'), and no one enters them except one who has been given permission to do so; rather their owners are appointed to keep people away from them. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya also said: He, exalted is He, intended the houses of Makkah, and this is according to the view that it is not owned (ghayr mutamallika), that people share in it, and that Makkah was taken by force ('anwatan).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, in this matter, is the weak opinion. It is refuted by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Did 'Aqil leave us any dwelling?" and his saying: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan," and whoever enters his house, and other aspects of reasoning.

The rest of the verse is clear; its apparent meaning is a warning (al-tawa'aud).

(p-373)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 30–31:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do.﴾ ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears of it, and let them draw their head-coverings (khumur) over their chests (juyub).﴾

His saying, ﴿Say to the believing men﴾, is equivalent to His saying "they". So His saying "yaghuddu" (they should lower) is the answer to the imperative. Al-Mazini said: the meaning is "Say to them: lower [your gaze], and they will lower [it]." Two objections arise against these two views. First, the answer is a statement from Allah, the Exalted, yet some people do not lower their gaze. This is resolved by saying that the intended meaning is: they are in the position of those who lower their gaze.

His saying, ﴿from their gaze﴾: the most apparent function of "min" (from) is that it expresses partiality (tab'id), because a person does not control the first glance. He lowers his gaze only after that, so partiality has occurred. This interpretation is supported by what is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him): "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours." (The hadith continues.) Jarir ibn 'Abdullah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about a sudden glance, and he said: "Turn your gaze away." It is also permissible that "min" be explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins), and it is also permissible that it indicates the starting point of the action (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The gaze is the greatest gateway to the heart, and the most thriving of the paths of the senses towards it. Accordingly, falling into sin through it is frequent, and a warning against it is obligatory.

"Guarding the private parts" may be understood as referring to protection from unlawful sexual intercourse (zina), and it may be understood as referring to covering the awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered). The most apparent view is that all of these are intended, and the wording is general. By this verse the scholars prohibited entering the bathhouse without a loincloth (mi'zar). Abu al-'Aliya said: every "private part" (furuj) mentioned in the Qur'an refers to unlawful sexual intercourse, except these two verses, for it means concealment.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view there is no basis for this restriction.

The rest of the verse is clear, and its apparent meaning is a threat.

His saying, ﴿And say to the believing women﴾, and the verse [continues]: In this verse Allah, the Exalted, commands women to lower their gaze from everything that the Sharia disapproves of looking at. In the hadith of Umm Salama, she said: "I and 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with them both) were with the Prophet (ﷺ), when Ibn Umm Maktum entered, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Veil yourselves.' We said: 'He is blind.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Are you two blind?'" The word "min" (from) may carry the same meaning as in the first [verse]. And "guarding the private parts" includes avoiding immoral acts, covering the awrah, and whatever is less than that which involves protection.

Allah, the Exalted, commanded that they not display their adornment to those who look, except what He excepted from among those who look in the rest of the verse. Then He excepted what [of the adornment] appears. People differed about the extent of this. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the apparent adornment is clothing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the face and clothing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said, as did 'Ata' and al-Awza'i: the face, the two palms, and clothing. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), Qatada, and al-Miswar ibn Makhrama said: the apparent adornment is kohl, the siwak (tooth-stick), henna dye up to half the forearm, earrings, and rings. Something like this is permissible for a woman to display to everyone who enters upon her from among the people. Al-Tabari mentioned from Qatada, concerning the meaning of half the forearm, a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and mentioned another from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It appears to me, from the wording of the verse, that the woman is commanded not to display [her adornment], and to strive in concealing everything that is adornment. The exception was made for whatever overcame her so that it appeared through the necessity of movement in what is unavoidable, or for the sake of an affair that needed attention, and similar things. What appears in this manner is what is pardoned. Most commonly, the face together with what it contains and the two palms are those from which exposure frequently occurs, and this is what is apparent in prayer. For a woman of good appearance it is commendable to cover herself, except before one who is forbidden to her by marriage-relationship. The wording of the verse allows that the apparent adornment may be displayed by her, but what we have said is strengthened by caution and by consideration of the corruption of people. So it should not be assumed that women are permitted to display adornment except that which is of this kind. And Allah is the One who grants success in what is correct, by His mercy.

The majority recited "walyadribna" with the lam of command vowelled with sukun. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Abbas from him, recited "waliyadribna" with the lam vowelled with kasra, according to the original form, because the original vowel of the lam of command is kasra, as in "liyadhhab" and "liyadrib." Its sukun is like the sukun in "'adud" and "fakhidh."

The occasion of revelation of this verse is that women in that time, when they covered their heads with the khimar, let it hang down behind the back. Al-Naqqash said: as the Nabateans do. Thus the throat, the neck, and the ears remained uncovered. So Allah, the Exalted, commanded them to wrap the khimar over the chests [juyub]. The manner of this is [that the woman strikes her khimar over her chest], so that it covers all that we have mentioned.

'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: May Allah have mercy on the first women emigrants (muhajirat). When this verse was revealed, they hastened to the thickest of their cloaks (murut), tore them into head-coverings (akhmira), and struck them over their chests. Hafsa bint Akhiha 'Abd al-Rahman entered upon 'A'isha, having covered herself with something transparent that showed her neck and what was around it, so 'A'isha tore it off her and said: "It is only to be struck with that which is thick and conceals."

The well-known reading is with a damma on the jim in "juyubihinna." Some of the Kufans read it with a kasra because of the following ya', like their reading of that in "buyut" and "shuyukh." This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi.

**

The words of the Exalted:

﴿And not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or those whom their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private matters.﴾

The meaning of this verse: they should not intend to abandon concealing the hidden adornment, such as anklets, earrings, and the like, and they should dispense with the burden of guarding it, except before those who are named. He began with the husbands (bu'ulah), who are the spouses, because their seeing falls upon something greater than this. Then he followed with the mahram relatives and equated them in the display of adornment. However, their ranks differ in sanctity according to what is in human souls. There is no doubt that the father's and the brother's seeing of the woman is more cautious than the seeing of her husband's son. The ranks of what is displayed to them also differ, so what may be displayed to the father is not what may be displayed to the husband's son.

His saying, ﴿or their women﴾, means all believing women, as if He had said: "or their kind." This includes believing slave women, and excludes women of polytheists, including the protected people (ahl al-dhimma) and others. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to Abu 'Ubayda (may Allah be pleased with him): "It has reached me that the women of the protected people enter the bathhouses with the women of the Muslims. Prevent that and stop it, for it is not permissible for a dhimmi woman to see the nakedness of a Muslim woman." He said: At that, Abu 'Ubayda stood, made supplication, and said: "Any woman who enters the bathhouse without an excuse, intending only to whiten her face, Allah will blacken her face on the Day when faces are whitened."

His saying, ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾, includes female slaves who are People of the Book, and it includes male slaves according to a group of the scholars. This is the apparent position of the school of 'A'isha and Umm Salama (may Allah be pleased with them both). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and a group of scholars said: a male slave does not enter upon his mistress and see her hair or the like, unless he is a menial servant (wagh). This group therefore prohibited uncovering before those possessed by the right hand, (p. 377) and permitted it for those who are "male attendants without physical desire." In some copies of the Mushaf there is "or those whom your right hands possess," which then includes the slave of another.

His saying, "or male attendants," means the followers (al-atba') who come to be fed the leftovers, and who are men with no physical desire for intercourse. These are two conditions. This description includes the castrated man (majbub), the mentally deficient (ma'tuh), the effeminate man (mukhannath), the aged decrepit man, and the disabled man incapacitated by his disability. Something like this is the usual case with these categories. Many an effeminate man should not be uncovered, do you not see the hadith about "Hit," when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade uncovering him before women after he described Badiya bint Ghaylan ibn Mu'attab? Consider what is related in the reports about the effeminate broker. Similarly, the foolish and the mentally deficient are among those who should not be uncovered. And men with no physical desire are few.

"Al-irbah" is the need for intercourse. Some exegetes expressed this by saying: it is the one who follows you wanting only food and what he eats. Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited "ghayr" with a fatha, and it is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the mention in "al-tabi'in," or an exception from "al-tabi'in." The rest recited "ghayri" with a kasra as an attribute (na't) of "al-tabi'in." The discussion of it is like the discussion of [the phrase] "ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim" [al-Fatiha: 7].

His saying, "or the child," is a collective noun with the meaning of the plural. It is said "tifl" as long as he has not reached puberty. "Yazhharu" means: they become aware of [women's private matters] through intercourse. The majority pronounce the waw in "'awrat" with sukun. It is reported from Ibn 'Amir that he read the waw with fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: most commonly the waw is with sukun, like "jawzat" and "bayḍat," because of the heaviness of the vowel on the waw and the ya'. Whoever recited with fatha did so according to the original form of "fa'lah" and "fa'lat."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 32:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may succeed﴾ [an-Nur: 31] ﴿And marry the single among you and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾

Al-Tabari narrated from al-Mu'tamir, from his father, who said: A Hadrami claimed that a woman made two silver bracelets and made a [bead of] jaz' (onyx/agate). She placed them on her shins, then passed by a group of people and struck the ground with her foot, so the anklet struck against the jaz' and made a sound. Then this verse was revealed. The hearing of this adornment is more stirring of desire than its display. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Makki, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no verse in the Book of Allah Most High with more pronouns than this one; it contains twenty-five pronouns referring to the believing women, in both the genitive and nominative cases. And 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited: "li-ya'lama ma surra min zinatihinna" (so that what is hidden of their adornment may be known).

Then the Exalted and Majestic commanded repentance in an unrestricted form. He restricted the repentance of the disbelievers in another verse by sincerity and by ceasing [from disbelief], and the repentance of the People of the Covenant by clarification, meaning by the command of Muhammad ﷺ. He commanded this repentance in an unrestricted, general form, from every matter, small and great.

Ibn 'Amir recited: "ayyuhu al-mu'minun" with a damma on the ha' of "ayyuhа" (ayyuhu). Its basis is that he treats the kha' as if it were part of the same word, so that the i'rab (grammatical case) of the vocative falls on it. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) considered this very weak. Some people pause on "ayyuhu" (ayyuh), and some pause on "ayyuha" with the alif. Abu 'Ali favoured pausing with the alif, because the reason for dropping it in connected speech is only its being unvocalised together with the unvocalised lam; so when one pauses, the reason is removed and the alif returns, just as the ya' returns when one pauses on "muhilli" in His saying: ﴿ghayra muhilli al-sayd﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. The difference we have mentioned regarding "ayyuha al-mu'minun" is likewise in "ya ayyuha al-sahir" and "ayyuha al-thaqalan".

As for His saying: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾, this address is to everyone who can conceive of marrying in some circumstance; so they are commanded to marry those who have no spouse, both men and women without spouses. The apparent meaning of the verse is that a woman may not marry except through a guardian (wali). "Ayyim" is said of a man and of a woman, and from it is the poet's saying:

"By Allah, how excellent are the sons of 'Ali, the single among them and the one who marries."

Because of the generality of this wording, a group said that this verse abrogates the ruling of His saying: ﴿The fornicatress marries none but a fornicator or a polytheist, and that is forbidden to the believers﴾ [an-Nur: 3]. His saying ﴿and the righteous among your servants﴾ means: for marriage. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "min 'abidikum" (from your male slaves), whereas the majority read "min 'ibadikum"; the meaning is one, except that the context of elevation through marriage supports the majority reading.

This command to marry varies according to the individual person: in one circumstance it may be conceived as obligatory, in another as recommended, and other than that, according to what is said about marriage.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, promised to enrich the poor who marry, seeking the pleasure of Allah concerning them and holding fast against His disobedience. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Seek wealth through marriage. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I wonder at one who does not seek wealth through marriage, when Allah Most High has said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾. al-Naqqash said: This verse is a proof against those who say that the judge separates the spouses if the husband is poor and unable to provide maintenance, because Allah said ﴿Allah will enrich them﴾ and did not say "He separates them".

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak inference. This verse is not a judgment concerning one who is unable to maintain a spouse; rather it is a promise of enrichment, just as Allah promised it together with separation in His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [an-Nisa: 130]. The breaths of Allah's mercy are hoped for in every state, and it is promised.

His saying ﴿All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ are two attributes corresponding to the meaning in which the statement occurs: that is, All-Encompassing in bounty, All-Knowing of the one who deserves expansion and enrichment.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 33:**

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And let those who find no means for marriage keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a writing (of manumission), write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾

"Istaʿaffa" (اسْتَعَفَّ) is on the pattern *istafʿala*, and its meaning is: he sought to be chaste (ʿafīf). In this verse Allah commands everyone who is prevented from marriage and cannot find it, for whatever reason he is prevented, to seek chastity. Then, since the most common obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth, He promised enrichment from His bounty. According to this interpretation, the command to chastity covers everyone who is prevented from marriage for whatever reason.

A group of exegetes (mufassirun) said: "nikāh" in this verse is the name of what is paid as a dowry and spent on the marriage, such as the covering and clothing for what one wraps oneself in and what one wears. What led them to this view is His saying: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾. So they thought that those commanded to chastity are only those who lack the wealth with which to marry. In this view there is a restriction of those commanded to chastity, and that is weak.

Then Allah commanded all the believers that whoever among them has a slave, and the slave seeks a writing (of manumission), and his master knows good in him, the master should write it for him. Al-Naqqash said: its occasion was that a slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā asked his master for the writing, and he refused. Makki said: he was Subayh al-Qibti, slave of Hatib ibn Abi Baltaʿa. The word "al-kitāb" (الكِتابَ) in the verse is a verbal noun like "al-qitāl" and "al-jilād" and similar verbal nouns of the pattern *fāʿala*. And "al-kitāba" (الكِتابَةُ) is on the pattern *fiʿāla*, from the viewpoint that he writes for himself, and this (the master) writes on his behalf.

People differed as to whether this command to write (the contract) is obligatory or recommended, on two views. The school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that it is recommended. ʿAtaʾ said: it is obligatory. This is the apparent meaning of the statement of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, to Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning Sirin, when Sirin asked for the writing and Anas hesitated. ʿUmar said to him: "Write it for him, or I will certainly strike you with the whip." This is also the view of ʿAmr ibn Dinar and al-Dahhak.

People differed over what is meant by "good" (khayr). One group said: it is wealth. They did not require a master to write (the contract) for a slave unless he knew that the slave had wealth from which he could pay, or from trade in it. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar and Salman that they refused to write the contract for two slaves who desired the writing and promised to beg from people. Each of them said to his slave: "Do you want to feed me the filth of people?" Malik said: it is said that "good" means strength and the ability to pay. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the good is truthfulness in promise, scarcity of lying, and fulfilment, even if the slave has no wealth. ʿUbayda al-Salmani said: the good is righteousness in religion. In his time this was the saying that preceded (the others).

The mukatab is a slave for as long as a single dirham remains owed on him, and the prohibition of freedom (ḥurmat al-ʿitq) only takes effect after payment. This is the view of the majority of the community. Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: when he has paid one third of the writing, he is a freed person (ʿatīq) and a debtor (gharīm). ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: emancipation applies to him with the first installment he pays.

As for His saying: ﴿and give them from the wealth of Allah﴾, the exegetes said: it is a command to every master of a mukatab to remit to the slave part of the amount of his writing. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, considered it best that this be a quarter of the writing. Al-Zahrawi said: this was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Masʿud considered it best to be a third of it. Qatada said: a tenth of it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, held that it should be from its first installments, hastening to good and fearing that (the slave) might not reach its last. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others held that the remission should be at the last installment. The reason for this is that if it is remitted from the first installment, the slave may often become unable (to pay), and then he and his wealth return to the master, and that remission returns to him. It resembles charity. This is the view of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held this matter to be recommended, and he did not set a limit to the amount of the remission. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, and others held the remission to be obligatory, to be enforced by the judge against the mukatab and his heirs.

Al-Hasan, al-Nakhaʿi, and Buraydah said: the address in His saying ﴿and give them from the wealth of Allah﴾ is to all people together, that they should give charity to the mukatabun and help them in freeing their necks. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to those in authority, that they should give the mukatabun their share from the wealth of zakat, and this is what His saying ﴿and for the captives﴾ includes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity, in order to seek the transitory goods of this worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Nur: 33] ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses explaining [the truth], and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

It is narrated that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul had a slave girl called Musaykah, and it was said: Mu'adhah. He would order her to commit fornication and to earn by it. She complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the verse was revealed concerning him and concerning those hypocrites who did his deed."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33] refers back to "the slave girls." That is because when the slave girl desires chastity, then it is possible and conceivable that the master may be compelling her, and it is possible that he be forbidden from compulsion. But if the slave girl does not desire chastity, then it is not conceivable that it be said to the master: "Do not compel her," because compulsion is not conceivable concerning her while she is desiring fornication. So this is a ruling concerning masters and slave girls in this condition. This view has escaped many of the exegetes. Some of them said: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33] refers back to [the unmarried (al-ayama)] in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And marry off the unmarried among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32]. Others said: this condition in His saying, may He be exalted, "if they desire" is nullified (mulgha), and similar views that are weak. And Allah is the One who grants success to what is correct, by His mercy.

As for "the transitory goods of this worldly life" (ʿarḍ al-ḥayāh al-dunyā) in this verse: it is that thing which the community (ummah) acquires by its private parts. And the meaning of the rest of the verse: ﴿indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful toward them﴾. The forgiveness and mercy may be conceived toward those compelled after repentance has occurred from that, so the meaning is: Forgiving toward whoever repents. Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Ibn Jubayr read: "la-hunna ghafurun rahim" with the addition of "lahunna" (for them).

Then He, may He be exalted, enumerated for the believers His blessings in what He sent down to them of the clear verses, and in what He set forth for them as examples of the peoples who passed before, so that they might guard against what those peoples fell into, and in what He mentioned for them of admonitions. The majority of readers read "mubayyanat" with a fatha on the ya', meaning: Allah made them clear and manifest. Al-Hasan, Talhah, 'Asim, and al-A'mash read "mubayyinat" with a kasra on the ya', meaning: they (the verses) made the truth clear and manifest.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 35:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass is as if it were a glittering star, lit from a blessed tree, an olive that is neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents parables for mankind, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

"Al-nūr" (light) in the speech of the Arabs means the illuminations perceived by sight, and it is used figuratively for meanings that are sound and manifest, so one says, "a speech that has light (nūr)," and from it is "the clear Book" (al-kitāb al-munīr), and from it is the saying of the poet:

﴿A lineage as if upon it from the sun of forenoon is light, and from the cleft of dawn a pillar.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, has nothing like unto Him, so it is clear that He is not like the perceived illuminations, and there remains no meaning for the verse except that He intended: Allah is the Possessor of the light of the heavens and the earth, that is, by His power their illuminations shone, their affairs were set right, and their creatures stood firm. So the statement is by way of fixing an image in the mind, as you say: the king is the light of the nation, that is, by him is the sustenance of its affairs and the soundness of its whole. The matter concerning the king is figurative, whereas concerning the attribute of Allah, exalted is He, it is pure literal truth; for He is the One who originated the existent things, and created the intellect as a guiding light, since the manifestation of existence came about through it, just as the manifestation of visible things came about through light. Blessed is Allah, there is no lord besides Him.

A group said: the implied meaning is "the religion of Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is "the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth." The first is more general in meanings and clearer upon reflection.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿa and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read "Allāhu nawwara" with a fatḥa on the nūn and the wāw shaddah and a fatḥa on the rāʾ, as a verb of the form fa"ala.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Jews delved into its interpretation and objected to Muhammad ﷺ, saying: "How is He the light of the earth and the heaven, with a distance between us and Him?" Then ﴿the parable of His light is like a niche﴾ was revealed, meaning: the matter is not as you supposed; rather, He is light in that He is the sustainer and creator and originator of everything. "The parable of His light is thus and thus."

The commentators differed as to whom the pronoun in "nūrihi" (His light) refers. Ka'b al-Aḥbār and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, that is, the parable of the light of Muhammad ﷺ. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it refers to the believers, and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "the parable of the light of the believers"; and it is narrated that in his reading it is "the parable of the light of the believer," and it is narrated that in it is "the parable of the light of one who believed in Him." Al-Ḥasan said: it refers to the Qur'an and faith. Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: according to these opinions, one pauses at His saying "and the earth."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are opinions in which the pronoun returns to one who has not been mentioned, and in which the intended meaning of the verse is cut off.

A group said: the pronoun in "nūrihi" refers to Allah, exalted is He. Then this group differed about the meaning of the light that is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, by the attribution of creation to the Creator, as you say: "the sky of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah." Some of them said: it is Muhammad ﷺ; some said: it is the believer; some said: it is faith and the Qur'an. These opinions are consistent, and the meaning proceeds smoothly with them. It is as if the Jews, when they interpreted "Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth" as meaning illumination, were told: it is not so; rather, He is light in that He is the sustainer and guide of everything. The parable of His light in Muhammad ﷺ, or in the believer, or in the Qur'an and faith, is like a niche, which is a non-piercing recess in the wall in which is placed the lamp or the like.

In these three opinions the correspondence of a part of the example to a part of what is exemplified proceeds consistently. According to the view of one who said, "the one exemplified is Muhammad ﷺ" — and this is the view of Ka'b al-Khayr — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the niche, or his breast; the lamp is prophethood and what is connected with it of his deeds and guidance; the glass is his heart; the blessed tree is revelation, and the angels, the messengers of Allah to him, and its connected cause; the oil is the proofs, demonstrations and signs that revelation contains.

According to the view of one who said, "the one exemplified is the believer" — and this is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b — the niche is his breast, the lamp is faith and knowledge, the glass is his heart, the tree is the Qur'an, and its oil is the proofs and wisdom that it contains. Ubayy said: he is then in the best of states, walking among people like a living man walking among the graves of the dead.

As for one who said, "the one exemplified is the Qur'an and faith," the construction of the statement is: the parable of His light — which is faith in the breast of the believer — in his heart is like a niche, that is, like this sentence. This view does not match the comparison as the first two do, because the niche does not correspond to faith.

(p-387) The verse may bear another meaning, in which there is no correspondence of a part of the example to a part of what is exemplified, but rather the comparison occurs as a whole to a whole, [namely that one intends: the parable of the light of Allah, which is His guidance, His perfection of the making of every creature, and His shining proofs upon the whole] is like this whole of light which you take for yourselves, in this quality which is the most eloquent attribute of light among people; that is, the parable of the light of Allah in clarity is like this which is the utmost of you, O mankind.

"Al-mishkāh" is a non-piercing recess in the wall; so said Ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn 'Iyad, and the majority of the exegetes. It gathers the light best, and the lamp within it gives more light than elsewhere. Mujāhid said: al-mishkāh is the pillar upon whose top the lamp is placed. Abū Mūsā said: al-mishkāh is the iron or lead piece in which the wick is placed inside the glass. Mujāhid also said: al-mishkāh is the iron hooks from which the lamp is hung. The first is the most sound of these opinions.

His saying, "in a glass," because it is a transparent body, in which the lamp is brighter than in other than glass. "Al-miṣbāḥ" is the wick with its fire. Al-Kisā'ī, as narrated from him by Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, inclined the alif of "mishkāh" so that he gave the kāf preceding it a kasra; and Naṣr ibn 'Āṣim read "fī zujājatin" with a fatḥa on the zāy, and "al-zujājah" likewise; it is a dialect.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿as if it were a glittering star﴾, that is, in brightness and illumination. This may bear two meanings: either that the glass is like that by the lamp, or that it is in itself so by its clearness and the excellence of its substance. This second interpretation is more eloquent in aiding the light. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "al-kawkab al-durrī" is Venus. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ read "durrī" with a ḍamma on the dāl and a shaddah on the yā'; for this reading there are two possibilities: either the star is attributed to al-durr (pearl) for its whiteness and clearness, or its origin is "durriʾ," hamzated from al-durraʾ, which means pushing, and the hamza was lightened. Ḥamza, Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim read "durriʾ" with the hamza; it is a fa"īl from al-durraʾ, in the sense that they push one another, or in the sense that in it is what removes its obscurity. The pattern fa"īl is not found among nouns except in the words "marīq" (for safflower) and "surriyyah" when derived from "sirr"; the grammarian Abū ʿAlī explained this reading, while others considered it weak. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī read "dirri'" on the pattern fi"īl with a kasra on the fā', from al-darʾ, and this is well-founded. Qatāda read "dar-riyy'a" with a fatḥa on the dāl and the hamza; Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is rare, and only "al-sikkīnah" with a shaddah on the kāf is preserved from it. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Abū Rajāʾ and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim read "darriyy" with a fatḥa on the dāl without hamza.

Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Ibn Wathhāb and ʿĪsā read "tūqadu" with a ḍamma on the tā', that is, the glass is kindled. Abū ʿAmr, the people of Kufa, al-Ḥusn and Ibn Muḥaysin read "tawaqqadu" with a fatḥa on the tā' and wāw, a shaddah on the qāf and a ḍamma on the dāl, that is, the glass. Abū ʿAmr also, and Ibn Kathīr, read "tawaqqadu" with a fatḥa on the tā' and dāl, that is, the lamp. ʿĀṣim, as narrated from him by Ismāʿīl, read "yūqadu" with a raised yā', meaning "the lamp is kindled." Abū al-Fatḥ said: al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Muḥaysin, Sallām and Qatāda read "yawaqqadu" with a fatḥa on the yā', wāw and the shaddah on the qāf, and a raised dāl; its origin is "yatawaqqadu."

His saying, "from a tree," that is, from the oil of a tree. "Al-mubārakah" is the one that is made to increase. The olive is among the greatest fruits in growth, in the continual spreading of branches, and in freshness, especially in al-Shām; and the pomegranate likewise, and observation confirms this. The saying of Abū Ṭālib lamenting Musāfir ibn Abī ʿAmr ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams:

﴿Would that I knew, Musāfir ibn Abī ʿAmr — and would that the grieving one would say it: blessed is the dead stranger, as the pomegranate and the olive are blessed.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾: the majority read both with a kasra as an attributive following "zaytūnah." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "lā sharqiyyatun wa lā gharbiyyatun" with a ḍamma. The commentators differed about its meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, as al-Ṭabarī related from him: its meaning is that it is a tree in a thick cluster that surrounds it, so it is not exposed from the direction of the east nor from the direction of the west.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This opinion, in my view, is not sound as transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both; for the actual existence of such a tree would require that its fruit not ripen.

al-Ḥasan said: this tree is not one of the trees of this world; rather it is an example that Allah, exalted is He, struck for His light; and had it been in this world, it would have been either eastern or western.

Ibn Zayd said: he meant that it is of the trees of al-Shām, because the trees of al-Shām are the best of trees and of the blessed land.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, ʿIkrima, Qatāda and others said: the meaning of His saying, ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾, is that it is in an open part of the earth, which the sun touches all day long, turning around it; so it is not purely of the east to be called eastern, nor purely of the west to be called western.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾, is hyperbole concerning one of its attributes, its beauty and excellence. The majority read "tamsasuhu" with a tā' above; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read it with a yā' below. His saying, ﴿light upon light﴾: that is, all of these are helpers by which this light that has been exemplified is completed; and at this point the example is complete.

Then, blessed and exalted is He, mentioned His guidance to His light for whom He wills of His servants and whom He makes happy, and mentioned His bounty in striking parables for the servants, so that they may take heed and reflect, leading to faith.

(p-390)

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah an-Nur, verses 36–37**

Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says:

﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾. ﴿Men whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, from establishing prayer and giving zakat (obligatory alms). They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾.

The letter *bā'* in "بُيُوتٍ" (*buyūt*, "houses") may be read with a *ḍammah* or a *kasrah*. Scholars differed over the word "فِي" (*fī*, "in") at the start of the verse. It was said to be connected to "مِصْباحٌ" (*miṣbāḥ*, "lamp") in the preceding verse. Abū Ḥātim said: It was also said to be connected to the later "يُسَبِّحُ" (*yusabbiḥu*, "He is glorified"). On this reading, one pauses at "عَلِيمٌ" (*ʿalīm*, "All-Knowing"). Al-Rummānī said: It is connected to "يُوقَدُ" (*yūqadu*, "is kindled").

People differed about the houses which Allah meant in His words, ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid said: They are the mosques dedicated to Allah Most High, which by custom are illuminated with that type of lamp. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: He meant Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). He called them "houses" because it contains separate places, some of which are partitioned from others. It is related that the custom of the Children of Israel in lighting Bayt al-Maqdis was extreme in their concern for it. The oil was selected and sealed in its containers, prepared with special care and sanctified, so that the lighting would not be done with anything else. Thus it was the brightest of the houses on earth. ʿIkrimah said: He meant the houses of faith in general, both mosques and homes, which are lit at night for prayer and for the study of knowledge. Mujāhid said: He meant the houses of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The author, Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Allah's words, ﴿therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾, strengthen the view that these are the mosques.

His words "أذِنَ" (*adhina*, "permitted") mean "commanded" and "decreed." The true meaning of *idhn* is knowledge and enablement without prohibition. If it is accompanied by a command and execution, it is stronger. As for "تُرْفَعَ" (*turfaʿa*, "be raised"), it was said that its meaning is "be built and elevated." Mujāhid and others said this. It is similar to Allah's words: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever builds a mosque from his wealth, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." There are hadiths on this meaning. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: Its meaning is that it is magnified and its status is raised. "Remembrance of His name" refers to prayer and worship, both in speech and in action.

Ibn Kathīr and ʿĀṣim read "يُسَبَّحُ" (*yusabbaḥu*) with a *fatḥah* on the doubled *bā'*. *"At your call, O Yazīd, a suppliant for a dispute..."*

That is, "a suppliant weeps for him." On the second reading, "رِجالٌ" is in the nominative, governed by the apparent verb "يُسَبِّحُ." It is narrated from Yaḥyā ibn Thābit that he read "تُسَبِّحُ" (*tusabbiḥu*) with a *tā'* on top.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He meant the two rakʿahs of Ḍuḥā and the ʿAṣr prayer. Many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: This verse was revealed about the people of the markets who, when they heard the call to prayer, abandoned every occupation and hastened to it. Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar saw the people of the markets coming towards the prayer and said: These are the ones whom Allah meant by His words, ﴿neither commerce nor sale distracts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾. This is also narrated from Ibn Masʿūd.

This was mentioned by al-Rummānī. Others said: Since they saw it is only used with an annexed noun, a *tā'* was attached to it as a substitute for the deleted letter, so it becomes "*iqāmah*." When they annex it, they delete the substitute because they do not need it, since the annexed noun and the noun it annexes act as one word.

Al-Ḥasan said it means the obligatory zakat on wealth. The "Day that causes fear," which Allah, Blessed and Exalted, mentioned, is the Day of Resurrection.

People differed over the turning of hearts and eyes: how is it? One group said: People will see the realities directly, so the hearts of doubters and those who hold to error will turn from their beliefs to belief in the truth as it truly is, and likewise the eyes. Another group said: It is a turning upon the embers of Hell, and the purpose of the verse is to describe the terror of the Day of Resurrection. As for the first view, it does not imply terror. As for the second, the turning upon the embers of Hell is not on the Day of Resurrection itself but after it. In my view, the meaning of the verse is that, because of its intense terror and its onset, hearts and eyes on that Day are agitated, anxious and turning: from hope of salvation to another hope, from fear of destruction to another fear, and from looking at one terror to looking at another. The Arabs use this meaning in wars and similar situations. From it is the poet's line:

*"Rather, your heart was in the wings of a bird."*

And from it is Bashshār's line:

*"As if his heart were a ball that leaps..."*

And this is abundant.

The Exalted's saying:

﴿So that God may reward them for the best of what they did, and increase them from His bounty. God provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one takes for water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing, and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full. God is swift at reckoning.﴾ ﴿Or they are like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds: darknesses, one above another. When he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. And whomever God does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾

The lam in His saying "liyajziyahum" (so that He may reward them) is connected to a implied verb whose estimated sense is: "they did that, and made themselves ready for that, and the like." It is also possible that it is connected to His saying "yusabbihu" (glorify). His saying "ahsana ma 'amilu" (the best of what they did) contains an elided noun, whose estimated sense is: "the reward for the best of what they did." Then the Mighty and Majestic promised them an increase from His bounty beyond what their deeds require. So the people of Paradise are always in increase. Then He mentioned that He provides for whom He wills, bestowing on him from His mercy what He wills, without reckoning or enumeration. Every bounty from God is without reckoning, and every recompense for a deed is by reckoning.

When God the Exalted, in what preceded in this verse, mentioned the state of faith and of the believers and His illumination of their hearts, He followed that by mentioning the disbelievers and their deeds. He gave them and their deeds two similitudes. The first of them describes the state of their deeds in the Hereafter, that they are neither beneficial nor useful. The second describes their state in this world, that they are in the utmost of misguidance and gloom, which He illustrated by what He mentioned of the extreme darkness in His saying "or like darknesses."

"As-sarab" (the mirage) is what shimmers from the air at midday in the wide open deserts, and deceives the one looking at it from afar into thinking it is water. It is named so because it flows away like water. Likewise are the deeds of the disbeliever: he thinks in his worldly life that they will benefit him. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, he finds them to be nothing. So they are like the mirage, which the thirsty viewer takes for water; when he heads towards it and exhausts himself reaching it, he finds nothing. "Al-qi'a" (the level ground) is the plural of qa', like jar and jiyra. Al-qa' is the lowest, flat stretch of land. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the one who withholds the zakat of livestock: "it will be laid down for them in a level ground, flat and smooth." It has also been said that qi'a is a singular noun meaning the same as qa'. Maslama ibn Muharib recited "bi-qi'at" (in level grounds, plural). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' (with a variant transmission) recited "adh-dhama'an" (the thirsty), with a fatha on the mim, dropping the vowel of the hamza onto the mim and omitting the hamza.

His saying "until when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing" means: nothing beneficial against thirst, or it means: nothing existing in general. By "came to it" is meant that he came to the place where he imagined it to be. It is also possible that the pronoun in "jaa'ahu" (came to it) refers to the mirage. Then in the speech there would be an omitted element, indicated by the context, whose estimated sense is: "likewise the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection will suppose his deed to be beneficial, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing." The pronoun may also refer to the deed indicated by His saying "their deeds," and the simile would be completed by His saying "water." On this interpretation the speech needs no omitted element, but the simile would then be concise and abbreviated, because the intended meaning is clear.

His saying "and he finds God with him" means: [He finds Him] with the recompenses. The pronoun in "'indahu" (with him) refers to the knowledge. The remainder of the verse is clear: it contains a warning, and "swiftness of reckoning" in that it is by knowledge with no effort involved.

His saying "or like darknesses" is coordinated with His saying "like a mirage." This last example includes a description of their deeds in this world, that is, that they are in misguidance and the like, in such a gathered darkness made of these things. Some people have held that in this example there are parts corresponding to parts of the thing being illustrated. They said: "the darknesses" are the corrupt deeds and false beliefs; "the deep sea" is the disbeliever's breast and heart; "lujjiyy" means possessing a "lujja," which is the bulk and depth of water, and the gathering of its water makes its darkness more intense; "the wave" is the misguidance or ignorance that overwhelms his heart, and the crooked thoughts; "the clouds" are his desire for disbelief, his turning away from faith, and what has been stained upon his heart.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is acceptable, but to posit this correspondence as necessary is not acceptable.

Sufyan ibn Husayn recited "aw ka-zulumatin" with a fatha on the waw. The majority of the seven readers recited "sahabun" with raf' and tanwin, and "zulumatun" (with raf'). Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Qunbul, recited "sahabun" with raf' and tanwin, and "zulumatin" with kasra, as a substitute for the first "zulumat." Ibn Abi Bazza from Ibn Kathir recited "sahabu" without tanwin, as an idafa (construct) with "zulumat."

His saying "idha akhraja yadahu lam yakad yaraha" (when he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it) is a phrase that implies an intensification of the darkness. People have differed over this phrase: does it imply that this man, presumed to be in these conditions and stretching out his hand, saw his hand, or did he not see it at all? One group said: he did not see it at all, because "kada" means "came close to," so it is as if he said: "when he stretches out his hand, he does not come close to seeing it," and this implies the negation of seeing altogether. Another group said: rather, he saw it after difficulty and hardship, when he was about not to see it. The reasoning for this is that when "kada" is accompanied by a negative particle, the verb following it is affirmed, and when it is not accompanied by one, the verb is negated.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is binding whenever the negative particle after "kada" enters upon the verb that follows it. You say "kada Zayd yaqum" (Zayd almost stood), and the standing is negated. When you say "kada Zayd alla yaqum" (Zayd almost did not stand), the standing is affirmed and realized. And you say "kada al-na'am yatir" (the ostrich almost flies), which implies the negation of flight for it. When you say "kada al-na'am alla yatir" (the ostrich almost does not fly), flight becomes necessary for it. When the negative particle is with "kada," the matter is open to interpretation: sometimes it affirms the action, and sometimes it negates it. You say "al-maflug la yakad yaskun" (the paralytic can hardly keep still): this is a correct sentence that implies the negation of stillness. And you say "rajul mutakallim la yakad yaskun" (a talkative man who hardly keeps quiet): this is a correct sentence that implies the affirmation of stillness after effort and rarely. From this is His saying: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had nearly not done so﴾ [al-Baqara 71]: a negation with "kada" implying the necessity of the slaughter. His saying in this verse, ﴿he can hardly see it﴾, is a negation with "kada" which, on one of the two interpretations, implies the negation of seeing. For this, and the like, Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "The verbs of approximation have another grammatical behaviour," meaning that they are subtle in their usage.

His saying: ﴿And whomever God does not give light, for him there is no light﴾. One group said: it means in this world, that is, whomever God does not guide, will not be guided. Another group said: it means in the Hereafter, that is, whomever God does not have mercy on, and does not illumine his state with pardon and mercy, for him there is no mercy. The first is clearer and more fitting to the wording of the verse. Moreover, these two are mutually implicated: the light of the Hereafter belongs only to whoever had his heart illuminated in this world and was guided. The Sharia has established that whoever dies upon his disbelief is not forgiven and not shown mercy.

The first is clearer and more fitting to the wording of the verse. Moreover, these two are mutually implicated: the light of the Hereafter belongs only to whoever had his heart illuminated in this world and was guided. The Sharia has established that whoever dies upon his disbelief is not forgiven and not shown mercy.

The Exalted's saying:

﴿So that God may reward them for the best of what they did, and increase them from His bounty. God provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one takes for water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing, and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full. God is swift at reckoning.﴾ ﴿Or they are like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds: darknesses, one above another. When he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. And whomever God does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾

The lam in His saying "liyajziyahum" (so that He may reward them) is connected to a implied verb whose estimated sense is: "they did that, and made themselves ready for that, and the like." It is also possible that it is connected to His saying "yusabbihu" (glorify). His saying "ahsana ma 'amilu" (the best of what they did) contains an elided noun, whose estimated sense is: "the reward for the best of what they did." Then the Mighty and Majestic promised them an increase from His bounty beyond what their deeds require. So the people of Paradise are always in increase. Then He mentioned that He provides for whom He wills, bestowing on him from His mercy what He wills, without reckoning or enumeration. Every bounty from God is without reckoning, and every recompense for a deed is by reckoning.

When God the Exalted, in what preceded in this verse, mentioned the state of faith and of the believers and His illumination of their hearts, He followed that by mentioning the disbelievers and their deeds. He gave them and their deeds two similitudes. The first of them describes the state of their deeds in the Hereafter, that they are neither beneficial nor useful. The second describes their state in this world, that they are in the utmost of misguidance and gloom, which He illustrated by what He mentioned of the extreme darkness in His saying "or like darknesses."

"As-sarab" (the mirage) is what shimmers from the air at midday in the wide open deserts, and deceives the one looking at it from afar into thinking it is water. It is named so because it flows away like water. Likewise are the deeds of the disbeliever: he thinks in his worldly life that they will benefit him. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, he finds them to be nothing. So they are like the mirage, which the thirsty viewer takes for water; when he heads towards it and exhausts himself reaching it, he finds nothing. "Al-qi'a" (the level ground) is the plural of qa', like jar and jiyra. Al-qa' is the lowest, flat stretch of land. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the one who withholds the zakat of livestock: "it will be laid down for them in a level ground, flat and smooth." It has also been said that qi'a is a singular noun meaning the same as qa'. Maslama ibn Muharib recited "bi-qi'at" (in level grounds, plural). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' (with a variant transmission) recited "adh-dhama'an" (the thirsty), with a fatha on the mim, dropping the vowel of the hamza onto the mim and omitting the hamza.

His saying "until when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing" means: nothing beneficial against thirst, or it means: nothing existing in general. By "came to it" is meant that he came to the place where he imagined it to be. It is also possible that the pronoun in "jaa'ahu" (came to it) refers to the mirage. Then in the speech there would be an omitted element, indicated by the context, whose estimated sense is: "likewise the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection will suppose his deed to be beneficial, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing." The pronoun may also refer to the deed indicated by His saying "their deeds," and the simile would be completed by His saying "water." On this interpretation the speech needs no omitted element, but the simile would then be concise and abbreviated, because the intended meaning is clear.

His saying "and he finds God with him" means: [He finds Him] with the recompenses. The pronoun in "'indahu" (with him) refers to the knowledge. The remainder of the verse is clear: it contains a warning, and "swiftness of reckoning" in that it is by knowledge with no effort involved.

His saying "or like darknesses" is coordinated with His saying "like a mirage." This last example includes a description of their deeds in this world, that is, that they are in misguidance and the like, in such a gathered darkness made of these things. Some people have held that in this example there are parts corresponding to parts of the thing being illustrated. They said: "the darknesses" are the corrupt deeds and false beliefs; "the deep sea" is the disbeliever's breast and heart; "lujjiyy" means possessing a "lujja," which is the bulk and depth of water, and the gathering of its water makes its darkness more intense; "the wave" is the misguidance or ignorance that overwhelms his heart, and the crooked thoughts; "the clouds" are his desire for disbelief, his turning away from faith, and what has been stained upon his heart.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is acceptable, but to posit this correspondence as necessary is not acceptable.

Sufyan ibn Husayn recited "aw ka-zulumatin" with a fatha on the waw. The majority of the seven readers recited "sahabun" with raf' and tanwin, and "zulumatun" (with raf'). Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Qunbul, recited "sahabun" with raf' and tanwin, and "zulumatin" with kasra, as a substitute for the first "zulumat." Ibn Abi Bazza from Ibn Kathir recited "sahabu" without tanwin, as an idafa (construct) with "zulumat."

His saying "idha akhraja yadahu lam yakad yaraha" (when he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it) is a phrase that implies an intensification of the darkness. People have differed over this phrase: does it imply that this man, presumed to be in these conditions and stretching out his hand, saw his hand, or did he not see it at all? One group said: he did not see it at all, because "kada" means "came close to," so it is as if he said: "when he stretches out his hand, he does not come close to seeing it," and this implies the negation of seeing altogether. Another group said: rather, he saw it after difficulty and hardship, when he was about not to see it. The reasoning for this is that when "kada" is accompanied by a negative particle, the verb following it is affirmed, and when it is not accompanied by one, the verb is negated.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is binding whenever the negative particle after "kada" enters upon the verb that follows it. You say "kada Zayd yaqum" (Zayd almost stood), and the standing is negated. When you say "kada Zayd alla yaqum" (Zayd almost did not stand), the standing is affirmed and realized. And you say "kada al-na'am yatir" (the ostrich almost flies), which implies the negation of flight for it. When you say "kada al-na'am alla yatir" (the ostrich almost does not fly), flight becomes necessary for it. When the negative particle is with "kada," the matter is open to interpretation: sometimes it affirms the action, and sometimes it negates it. You say "al-maflug la yakad yaskun" (the paralytic can hardly keep still): this is a correct sentence that implies the negation of stillness. And you say "rajul mutakallim la yakad yaskun" (a talkative man who hardly keeps quiet): this is a correct sentence that implies the affirmation of stillness after effort and rarely. From this is His saying: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had nearly not done so﴾ [al-Baqara 71]: a negation with "kada" implying the necessity of the slaughter. His saying in this verse, ﴿he can hardly see it﴾, is a negation with "kada" which, on one of the two interpretations, implies the negation of seeing. For this, and the like, Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "The verbs of approximation have another grammatical behaviour," meaning that they are subtle in their usage.

His saying: ﴿And whomever God does not give light, for him there is no light﴾. One group said: it means in this world, that is, whomever God does not guide, will not be guided. Another group said: it means in the Hereafter, that is, whomever God does not have mercy on, and does not illumine his state with pardon and mercy, for him there is no mercy. The first is clearer and more fitting to the wording of the verse. Moreover, these two are mutually implicated: the light of the Hereafter belongs only to whoever had his heart illuminated in this world and was guided. The Sharia has established that whoever dies upon his disbelief is not forgiven and not shown mercy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 41–42:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight? Each has known its prayer and its glorification. And Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return.﴾

"Have you not seen" is an alert (tanbih), and "seeing" here is the seeing of reflection (ru'yat al-fikr). Sibawayh said: it is as if he said, "Pay attention: Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens..." And "tasbih" (glorification) here means exalting and declaring Allah free of imperfection. It applies to rational beings through speech and through prayer, from every possessor of religion. People differed regarding the glorification of birds and other things for which the Book has stated that they glorify. The majority hold that it is true glorification. Al-Hasan and others said it is a figurative expression, and that its glorification is in the manifestation of wisdom in it, so it, for that reason, calls to glorification.

The commentators said: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is general for everything, those who possess intellect and the rest of the inanimate things. But since they are gathered together, it is expressed by "man" (who), giving precedence to the ruling of those who have intellect. "Saffat" means: arranged in rows in the air. Al-A'raj read "wa-al-tayr" with a fatha on the ra', and al-Hasan read "wa-al-tayru saffatun" in the nominative.

As for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾, al-Hasan said: the meaning is that each has known the prayer of its own self and the glorification of its own self, so it persists in them and performs them. Mujahid said: prayer belongs to humans and glorification to others. Another group said: the meaning is that each has known the prayer of Allah and the glorification of Allah, which He commanded them with and guided them to; this is the attribution of a creature to its Creator. Al-Zajjaj and others said: the meaning is that each—Allah has known its prayer and its glorification, so the pronouns refer to "each." A group read "'ulima salatuhu wa-tasbihuhu" with a damma and the verb in the passive form whose subject is not named; Abu Hatim mentioned it. The majority read "yaf'alun" with a ya', for the sake of emphasis in describing the power of Allah and His knowledge of His creation. Isa and al-Hasan read "taf'alun" with a ta' from above; in it is the meaning mentioned plus the addition of warning and intimidation from Allah the Exalted, and an announcement afterward that dominion absolutely belongs to Him, and a reminder of the matter of the return to Him and the gathering strengthens the matter of being cautioned by Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, and of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "wa-Allahu basirun bi-ma taf'alun" (And Allah is Seeing of what you do).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 43–44:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them a heaped mass, so that you see the rain come out from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail wherein is [hail], so He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿He alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight.﴾

"Seeing" (al-ru'yah) in this verse is seeing with the eye, and the implied meaning is: [Have you not considered] that the command of Allah and His power [...]. "Yuzjī" means: He drives. Izjā' (driving) is used only for driving and pushing something heavy, such as clouds and camels in a slow-moving caravan, as al-Farazdaq said:

"... upon slow-moving camels that are driven by exhausted ones"

And "al-biḍā'ah al-muzjāh" (the goods that are poor) are those that need intercession and embellishment to be of the kind that must be driven like a heavy load. From this is the saying of Habib about gray hair: "and we drive it" [i.e., we drive it along]. Sibawayh always says in his speech: "fa-anta tuzjīhi ilā kadhā," meaning you drive it heavily and slowly toward such-and-such.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then joins them together﴾ means: joins together the scattered parts of the cloud itself; because the very concept of a cloud implies that there are gaps between it [its parts], and this is like when you say: "I sat between the houses." If "between" (bayn) is attached to a singular noun, it is not correct unless you mean another [thing]. You do not say "I sat between the house" unless you mean "and between such-and-such."

Warsh, from Nafi', does not hamz "yu'allifu," while Qalun, from Nafi', and the rest hamz "yu'allifu," which is the original form.

"Rukām" is that in which parts ride upon one another and become dense. The Arabs say: when Allah Exalted makes the cloud a heaped mass by the wind, He squeezes one part against another, and the rain comes out of it. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We send down from the squeezing clouds pure water﴾ [al-Naba' 14], and from this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"Both are the pressings of the grape-juice, so pour me [a cup] with a flask whose [contents] loosen the joint more."

It is also narrated as "lil-mifsal" with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the sad; al-mifsal is the singular of the joints (mafāṣil), and al-mifsal is the tongue. It is also narrated with a qaf. Hassan meant the wine and the water that was mixed with it: this is from the pressing of grapes, and this is from the pressing of the clouds. This explanation was given by the judge of Basra, 'Abdullah ibn al-Hasan, to a group whose companion had sworn by divorce that he would ask the judge about the explanation of Hassan's verse.

"Al-wadq" is rain, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Then no cloud has poured its pouring, nor has any land brought forth its vegetation."

The majority of readers recite "min khilālihi," which is the plural of khalal, like jabal and jibāl. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "min khalalihi." 'Āṣim and al-A'raj recited "wa-yunazzilu" with intensification, while the majority read it with lightening.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿mountains of hail wherein is [hail]﴾. It has been said: this is literal, and Allah Exalted has placed in the sky mountains of hail. Another group said: this is figurative, and it only intends to describe its abundance. This is like when you say: "With so-and-so are mountains of wealth, and mountains of knowledge," meaning in abundance like mountains. It is reported from al-Akhfash that his estimation is that "min" is extra in His saying "min barad," but this is a weak opinion. The "min" in His saying "min al-samā'" is for the starting point of the limit; in His saying "min jibāl" it is partitive; and in His saying "min barad" it is explanatory of the kind.

"Al-sanā" (with short vowel, maqṣūr) is light, and "al-sanā'" (extended, mamdūd) is glory and elevation in rank. The majority read "sanā" with the short form, while Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "sanā'a" with the extension and hamza. Ṭalḥa also read "buraqihi" with a damma on the ba' and a fatha on the ra', which is the plural of burqah (with a damma on the ba' and a sukun on the ra'), a fu'lah form, meaning a measure of lightning, like luqmah and luqam, and ghurfah and ghurof. The majority read "yadhhabu" with a fatha on the ya', while Abu Ja'far read "yudhhabu" with a damma, from adhhaba, as if the sense were: it takes away souls by sights, similar to His saying: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun 20]. It may also be like His saying: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj 25], where the ba' is extra, indicating a verb that suits it.

Then the words of the verse have required the report about the alternation of night and day, and the bringing of this after that without preparation. This is what eloquent speakers are unable to match, until they resort to refining the wording and preparing the speech. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 45–50:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And Allah has created every creature from water; of them are those that move on their bellies, and of them are those that walk on two legs, and of them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills; indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down distinct signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger and have obeyed"; then a faction of them turn away after that. And those are not believers.﴾ ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he might judge between them, at once a faction of them are turning away.﴾ ﴿But if the truth had been theirs, they would have come to him willingly, submitting.﴾ ﴿Is there in their hearts disease, or have they come to doubt, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾

This is a verse of reflection (i'tibar). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-Allahu khaliqu kulli" (with the genitive construction), while the majority read "wa-Allahu khalaqa kulla" (with the verb). "Al-dabba" (the creature) is everything that crawls (yadibbu) among animals, i.e., that moves, progressing forward step by step. It includes birds, since they too may crawl. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿...................﴾ "the crawling of the sand-grouse of al-Batha in every watering place."

It also includes fish. In a hadith: "A creature from the sea, like the zarab (a kind of lizard)." As for His saying "from water," al-Naqqash said: it means the sperm of males. The majority of the reflective scholars (jumhur al-nazra) said: it means that the making of every animal contains water, just as Adam was created from water and clay. On this basis is explained the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the old man who asked during the battle of Badr, "From whom are you two?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "We are from water," the hadith.

Walking on the belly is for snakes, fish, and similar worms and others; walking on two legs is for humans and birds when they walk; and on four for the rest of animals. In the Codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "and of them are those that walk on many (akthar)," thereby including all animals by this addition. However, it is a Qur'an that consensus (ijma') has not established. Yet al-Naqqash said: the speech suffices by mentioning what walks on four rather than what walks on many, because the basis of the movement of all animals is on four, which is the foundation of their walking, and the multiplicity of legs in some of them is an addition to their creation that the animal does not need in order to walk with all of them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning is that those many legs are not vain; rather, the animal has need of them in its movement, and each of them moves in its conduct.
