Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 24, verses 51–54:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey." And those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, and fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him, those are the attainers of success.﴾ ﴿And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if you were to order them, they would certainly go forth. Say, "Do not swear; [your] obedience is known. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do."﴾ ﴿Say, "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon him is only that which he has been assigned, and upon you is that which you have been assigned. And if you obey him, you will be [rightly] guided. And there is not upon the Messenger except clear notification."﴾

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "qawla" (قَوْلَ) with a fatḥa, while ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "qawlu" (قَوْلُ) with a ḍamma, and reports differ concerning the latter two. Abū al-Fatḥ said: the condition of "kāna" (كانَ, "was") is that its subject be more definite than its predicate, so the reading of the majority is stronger. The meaning is: "The obligation upon the believers, when they are called to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, is that they should say, 'We hear and we obey.'" Thus this "kāna" is not a report about the past; it is like the saying of the Companion (al-Ṣiddīq, raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "It was not for the son of Abū Quḥāfa to lead the prayer in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." And the calling to Allah has been treated as calling to His law and His religion.

The majority read "liyaḥkuma" (لِيَحْكُمَ) with the verb in the active voice, while Abū Jaʿfar, al-Jaḥdarī, Khālid ibn Ilyās, and al-Ḥasan read "liyuḥkama" (لِيُحْكَمَ) with the verb in the passive voice. "Al-mufliḥūn" (الْمُفْلِحُونَ) means: those who attain their hopes in their worldly life and their Hereafter.

"Jahd al-yamīn" (جَهْدُ اليَمِينِ) means exerting oneself to the utmost in making the oath binding. "Layakhrujunna" (لَيَخْرُجُنَّ) means: "to the expedition (ghazw)." This [verse] concerns the hypocrites who turned away when they were called to Allah and His Messenger. His saying: ﴿Say, "Do not swear; [your] obedience is known"﴾ may carry several meanings:

First: a prohibition against false oaths, since it is known that their obedience is corrupt and wretched, so it is as if He says: "Do not deceive; He knows what you are upon."

Second: the meaning is: "Do not burden yourselves with oaths; moderate obedience according to your capacity is better and more beneficial for you." In this interpretation there is also a kind of leniency toward them.

Third: the meaning is: "Do not be content with oaths; obedience that is recognized from you and visible upon you is what is required of you."

Fourth: the meaning is: "Do not persuade yourselves that you have pleased us with oaths; the obedience of Allah is well known, and His law and the striving against His enemy are clear and evident."

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿Do not swear﴾, and ﴿[your] obedience is known﴾ is an eloquent parenthetical interjection.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say, "Obey Allah"﴾ and the verse that follows address those hypocrites and others among the disbelievers, and everyone who is arrogant toward the command of Muḥammad ﷺ. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 55–57:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿God has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land, as He made successors of those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely give them, in place of their fear, security. They worship Me, not associating anything with Me. And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And establish prayer, give zakah, and obey the Messenger that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will cause failure [to Allah] within the land. And their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination.﴾

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "istukhlifa" (ustukhlifa) with the verb in the passive form. It is narrated that the cause of this verse was that some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ complained of the hardship of fighting the enemy and of the fear they were in for their own selves, and that they could not lay down their weapons. So this verse was revealed in general terms for the community of Muhammad ﷺ.

His saying, Exalted is He, "in the land" means: in the lands adjacent to them and the regions to which their expansion was decreed to reach. Their being made successors means that He grants them dominion over the lands and makes them its people, as occurred in al-Sham, Iraq, Khurasan and the Maghrib. Al-Dahhak said, in the Kitab al-Naqqash: this verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all, because they are people of faith and righteous deeds. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The caliphate after me will be thirty years."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view regarding the verse is that it concerns the successorship of the community as a whole.

The lam in His saying, Exalted is He, "la-yastakhlifannahum" is the lam of oath. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-li-yubaddilannahum" with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the dal. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal. Regarding the meaning of the change of their fear into security, it is reported that when the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said, "Will there not come upon us a day when we are secure and lay down our arms?", the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You will not be troubled except for a little, until a man among you sits in a great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon in it." His saying, "they worship Me" is a resumptive clause, meaning: they worship Me. His saying, "And whoever disbelieves" means: disbelieves these blessings once they have come about. Based on this, the defiance (fisq) is not one that removes one from the religion. Some people said in the book of al-Tabari: this appeared among the murderers of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also possible that it means disbelief and defiance that remove one from the religion, and this is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, for he said: "During the time of the Prophet ﷺ there was hypocrisy, and it has gone; there remains only disbelief after faith."

Since He had earlier mentioned the doing of righteous deeds, He explained them in this verse, specifying their greatest parts, which are establishing prayer and giving zakah, and generalized with obedience to the Messenger, because it encompasses all acts of obedience. And "la'allakum" means: with respect to you and your belief.

Then He turned his speech against the disbelievers by alerting that they are not escaping the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He.

The majority of the seven readers read "la tahsabanna" with the ta', addressing the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the sin. Hamza and Ibn 'Amir read "la yahsabanna" with the ya'. Abu 'Ali said: this allows two possibilities: the first is that the implied subject is Muhammad (the verb being "do not let Muhammad think"); the second is that the verb is attributed to those who disbelieve, with the object being themselves. And a man "a'jaza" when he goes off in the land and is not overtaken. Then He informed that their refuge is the Fire, and that it is a wretched end and destination.

It is narrated that the cause of this verse was that some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ complained of the hardship of fighting the enemy and of the fear they were in for their own selves, and that they could not lay down their weapons. So this verse was revealed in general terms for the community of Muhammad ﷺ.

His saying, Exalted is He, "in the land" means: in the lands adjacent to them and the regions to which their expansion was decreed to reach. Their being made successors means that He grants them dominion over the lands and makes them its people, as occurred in al-Sham, Iraq, Khurasan and the Maghrib. Al-Dahhak said, in the Kitab al-Naqqash: this verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all, because they are people of faith and righteous deeds. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The caliphate after me will be thirty years."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view regarding the verse is that it concerns the successorship of the community as a whole.

The lam in His saying, Exalted is He, "la-yastakhlifannahum" is the lam of oath. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-li-yubaddilannahum" with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the dal. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal. Regarding the meaning of the change of their fear into security, it is reported that when the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said, "Will there not come upon us a day when we are secure and lay down our arms?", the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You will not be troubled except for a little, until a man among you sits in a great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon in it." His saying, "they worship Me" is a resumptive clause, meaning: they worship Me. His saying, "And whoever disbelieves" means: disbelieves these blessings once they have come about. Based on this, the defiance (fisq) is not one that removes one from the religion. Some people said in the book of al-Tabari: this appeared among the murderers of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also possible that it means disbelief and defiance that remove one from the religion, and this is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, for he said: "During the time of the Prophet ﷺ there was hypocrisy, and it has gone; there remains only disbelief after faith."

Since He had earlier mentioned the doing of righteous deeds, He explained them in this verse, specifying their greatest parts, which are establishing prayer and giving zakah, and generalized with obedience to the Messenger, because it encompasses all acts of obedience. And "la'allakum" means: with respect to you and your belief.

Then He turned his speech against the disbelievers by alerting that they are not escaping the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He.

The majority of the seven readers read "la tahsabanna" with the ta', addressing the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the sin. Hamza and Ibn 'Amir read "la yahsabanna" with the ya'. Abu 'Ali said: this allows two possibilities: the first is that the implied subject is Muhammad (the verb being "do not let Muhammad think"); the second is that the verb is attributed to those who disbelieve, with the object being themselves. And a man "a'jaza" when he goes off in the land and is not overtaken. Then He informed that their refuge is the Fire, and that it is a wretched end and destination.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 58:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not reached puberty among you ask permission of you three times: before the prayer of dawn, and when you put aside your clothing at midday, and after the prayer of night. Three times of nakedness for you. There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they go around attending you, some of you to others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him both) said: "Those whom your right hands possess" is meant specifically for males. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: it is meant specifically for females, and the way for males is that they should ask permission at every time. Al-Zahrawi related from Abu 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him both) something similar to this. It has also been said: men and women are both intended in their entirety, and al-Tabari preferred this view. The majority of readers ("al-nas") read "al-hulum" with a damma on the lam, while al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "al-hulm" with a sukun on the lam. Abu 'Amr used to find this reading good.

This verse is muhkam (clear and definitive, not abrogated). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) said: "People have abandoned it, just as people have abandoned His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]; people refuse except that the most noble is the most fitting."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This expression, "abandoned by the people," is an intensification and a rebuke, since it is not adhered to with full adherence. Otherwise, what Allah the Exalted said is the belief among the scholars recorded in their writings: that nobility is piety. As for the matter of seeking permission, the change in building structures and screens has made much of seeking permission unnecessary and has placed it on a different footing. Where are the doors of homes today relative to the places of sleep? Al-Mahdawi related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) that he said: "The acting upon this verse was obligatory when they had no locks and no doors; if the situation returned, the obligation would return."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

So it is now obligatory in many of the dwellings of the Muslims in the deserts, the open lands, and the like.

According to a group of scholars, the meaning of the verse is that Allah the Exalted disciplined His servants by requiring that the slaves (since they have no concern of the private parts, as it were) and the children who have not reached puberty, but who understand the meanings of nakedness and the like, should ask permission to enter upon their family in these three times. These are the times when the customary habit of people requires exposure and staying in a state of undress in beds: at dawn, because people at that time are naked in their beds, and a sleeper may become uncovered, so whoever walks in and enters and exits should ask permission lest he see what must be covered; likewise at the time of midday rest (al-qa'ilah), which is noon, because the day becomes apparent in it when it rises and its heat intensifies; and after the night prayer ('isha'), because it is the time of undressing for sleep and changing into bedclothes. As for other times, which are not times of exposure ('awrah, i.e., times of uncovering), the custom of people is caution and guardedness, so there is no blame in entering this category without permission, since they are attendants who come and go, and people find no escape from this.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "tawwafin" with a ya'. Al-Hasan said: if a man lodges his servant with him, there is no need for him to ask permission even during these three times.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿some of you to others﴾, are a substitution (badal) for His saying "attendants" (tawwafun). And ﴿three times of nakedness﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), because they were not commanded to ask permission three times; rather they were commanded to ask permission at three occasions, so the adverbial sense in "three" is clear.

The majority of the seven readers read "thalathu 'awrat" with "thalath" in the nominative, and likewise as the subject of a nominal sentence. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "thalatha 'awrat" with "thalath" in the accusative. This is in apposition (badal) to the time-adverb in His saying "thalatha marrat." This apposition is only correct in meaning by taking the sense: "times of three nakednesses," so the first noun is omitted and the second noun put in its place. "'Awrat" is the plural of "'awrah," and its regular pattern in the sound form is "fa'alat" with a fatha on the 'ayn, as in "jafnah" and "jafanat" and the like. For the weak (doubled or hollow) form they made the 'ayn sukun, as in "baydah" and "baydat," "jawbah" and "jawbat," and the like, because a fatha there would lead to its weakness, so it was not given a fatha for that reason.

The commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Nūr, verses 59–60:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them for putting aside their outer garments, provided they do not display adornment. But that they refrain is better for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

The meaning is that the children were commanded to ask permission at the three times mentioned, and it was permitted for them to enter at other times besides these. Then Allah, exalted is He, commands in this verse that when they reach puberty they are to be under the ruling of men regarding seeking permission at every time. This is a clarification from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

And "al-qawāʿid" (the women past child-bearing) refers to the women who have grown old and have ceased to bear children; the singular is qāʿid. Rabīʿa said: here it refers to those who are found repulsive because of their age. Others said: a woman may cease to bear children while still being an object of desire. Since it is generally the case with women of this age that men have no interest in them, they were granted what was not granted to others, and the burden of the strict, wearisome covering was removed from them, since the cause of covering is absent in them. Ibn Masʿūd read: "an yaḍaʿna min thiyābihinna" (that they put aside some of their garments), and this is the reading of Ubayy. It is also narrated from Ibn Masʿūd: "min jalābībihinna" (of their outer cloaks). The Arabs say "imraʾatun wāḍiʿ" (a woman who has put down) for a woman who has grown old and removed her head-cover. Then a condition was stipulated upon them regarding the putting aside of garments: that they not intend thereby display (tabarruj) and the showing of adornment, for many an old woman may show a desire to appear attractive, and similar things, which are among the most reprehensible matters and furthest from the truth.

Tabarruj is the seeking to be seen and to appear. From it comes "burūjin mushayyadah" (towers built high). The origin of this is the towers of the sky and the walls. What is permitted for this category to put aside is the outer cloak worn over the head-cover, and the wrapper; this was said by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Jubayr, and others.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that the restraint of all of them, their chastity in refraining from putting aside garments, and their adherence to what young women adhere to of covering, is better and more excellent for them. Ibn Masʿūd read: "wa-an yataʿaffafna" (and that they be chaste), without the sīn. Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He is All-Hearing of what every speaker, male and female, says, and All-Knowing of the intention of each person in their words; and in these two attributes there is a warning and a caution. And Allah is the One who grants success to what is right, by His mercy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 61:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your own houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately.  So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, that you may understand.﴾

People have differed about the meaning by which Allah lifted the blame from these three categories. The apparent meaning of the verse and the purpose of the Shari'ah is that blame is lifted from them in everything to which their excuse compels them, and their intention calls for them to perform the most complete form of it, while their excuse entails that what occurs from them is the lesser. So blame is lifted from them in this matter. As for what people have said about "blame" here: Ibn Zayd said: it is the blame of going out to battle, meaning there is no blame upon them for staying behind. His words, ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾ and so on, are a separate meaning cut off from the first. Another group said: the whole verse concerns food. They said: the Arabs and those in Madina before the Prophethood (ﷺ) would avoid eating with people of excuses. Some of them did this out of disgust at the wandering of the hand of the blind man, the spreading out of the lame man's sitting, and the smell and ailments of the sick. These are jahili manners and arrogance, so the verse came to discipline them. Others did it out of scruple toward people without excuses, since those with excuses were restricted in eating compared to the healthy, due to the blind man's inability to see, the lame man's inability to compete, and the sick man's weakness, so the verse came permitting eating with them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the book of al-Zahrawi: if the people of these excuses scrupled to eat with others because of their excuse, the verse came permitting them.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: the verse, from its beginning to its end, was revealed because when the verse ﴿and do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] was revealed, people said: there is no wealth more precious than food. They scrupled that anyone should eat with these people and thereby take advantage of them in eating, falling into consuming wealth falsely. Likewise they scrupled to eat the food of relatives for this reason. So the verse came permitting all of these foods, and clarifying that the prohibition applies only to transgression, gambling, and everything a person eats from another's property when the other dislikes it, or in a corrupt manner, or the like.

'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba ibn Mas'ud said: His words concerning the three categories were revealed because people, when they set out for battle, left behind those of excuse in their homes and property, and those of excuse would avoid eating the property of the absent. So the verse came permitting them to eat what they need from the food of the absent, when the absent person had been content with that.

It was also said: when a man brought people of excuse to his house and found nothing in it, he would take them to the house of a relative, and the people of excuse scrupled at this, so the verse was revealed.

Allah mentioned the houses of relatives and omitted the houses of children. The commentators said: this falls under His words ﴿from your houses﴾, because a man's son's house is his house. Talha ibn Musarrif read "immahatikum" with a kasra on the hamza.

His words ﴿or from that whose keys you possess﴾ mean what you have acquired and what has come into your possession. It includes what a man owns in his house and under his lock. This is the interpretation of al-Dahhak and Mujahid. According to the majority of commentators, stewards, slaves, and hired workers in accordance with what is customary are included in the verse. The majority of people read "malaktum" with a fatha on the mim and lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "mallaktum" with a damma on the mim, a kasra on the lam, and shadda. The majority read "mafatihahu". Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "mafatiyahu", with a ya between the ta' and the ha', the first being the plural of miftah... [the plural forms as in the source]. Qatada read "malaktum mafatihahu".

In this verse Allah paired the friend with the pure and firm kinship, because the nearness of affection is intimate. Ma'mar said: I said to Qatada, "Shall I not drink from this well?" He said: "You are my friend, so what is this seeking of permission?" Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the book of al-Naqqash: the friend is more emphatic than kinship. Do you not see in the cry for help of the people of Hell: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100] ﴿nor a close friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 101].

His words ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾ are a refutation of the view of a group of Arabs who never ate alone at all, as al-Tabari said. From this is the saying of one of the poets:

When you prepare the provision, then seek for it a companion, for I do not eat it alone.

Some Arabs, when they had a guest, would not eat unless they ate with their guest. So this verse came clarifying the sunnah of eating and removing everything contrary to it from the custom of the Arabs, and permitting the solitary eating of what was forbidden among the Arabs. It leaned toward generosity of character and went to excess in obligating it, though bringing a companion to the meal is good, provided that eating alone is not made unlawful.

Some of the scholars said: this verse is abrogated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed your blood and your property are sacred to you," and by His words: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 27], and by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "No one shall milk another's livestock except with his permission," the hadith.

Then Allah concluded the verse by clarifying the sunnah of greeting in houses. People differed as to which houses were meant. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it means the mosques, and the meaning is: greet those in them of your kind. This is like His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. If there is no one in the mosques, the greeting is for a person to say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah." It was also said: he says, "Peace be upon you," intending the angels, then he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." His words "tahiyyatan" are a verbal noun, and it is described as blessed because in it is supplication and the drawing of the affection of the Muslim to whom it is addressed. The kaf in His words "kadhalika" is the kaf of comparison, and "dhalika" is a reference to these sunan, meaning: what He has described is consistently how He makes the signs clear, so that you may understand them and act upon them.

Some people said regarding this verse that it is abrogated by the verse of seeking permission, which people were commanded to observe, and which is mentioned earlier in the surah. For if permission is prohibited, food is all the more so. Likewise, a group proposed abrogation between it and His words: ﴿and do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abrogation is not conceivable in any of these verses; rather, they are all muhkam (definitive). As for His words ﴿and do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188], it concerns transgression, deception, fraud, frivolity, gambling, and the like. As for this verse, it concerns the permission of the food of these categories, whose being fed in this manner pleases them. As for the verse of permission, the reason for the obligation of seeking permission is fear of exposing what is private; so when a man seeks permission, having dispelled the fear of exposure, and enters the house in the permitted manner, it is valid for him afterward to eat the food under this permission. There is no abrogation in the verse, so reflect upon it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verse 62:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Only those are the believers who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whom you will among them and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

"Innama" (only) in this verse indicates restriction (hasr), and this meaning is required, because faith is not complete except by a person believing in Allah and His Messenger, and by being attentive to the Messenger, not being obstinate about what the Messenger ﷺ wishes to command, so that he does not wish to corrupt it by leaving at the time of the gathering and the like.

The "matter of common concern" (al-amr al-jami') refers to that for which the leader (al-imam) needs to gather the people in order to proclaim a benefit (maslaha). The obligatory etiquette of Islam in this regard, when the matter is present, is that no one leaves for an excuse except with his permission. If he leaves with permission, the bad suspicion is removed from him. The leader whose permission is awaited in this verse is the leader of command (imam al-imara). Makhul and al-Zuhri said: Friday prayer is among the matters of common concern, and the imam of the prayer should ask permission when the leader of command has delegated him, if he sees the one asking. Some people for a long time followed the practice of asking permission of the imam of the prayer. It is narrated that Haram ibn Hayyan was delivering a sermon, when a man stood up, placed his hand over his nose, and gestured to Haram to ask permission, and he granted it. When the prayer was finished, it was revealed that he had only left without necessity. Haram said: "O Allah, delay the men of evil until the time of evil."

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that permission must be sought from the commander-in-chief who occupies the station of prophethood, for he may have an opinion about detaining that man for a matter of the religion. As for the imam of the prayer alone, that is not his to decide, for he is a deputy over one part of the religion on behalf of the one who occupies the station of prophethood.

(p-414) Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to give permission to whoever he recognized as having a genuine excuse, and they are "whom he wills."

It is narrated that this verse was revealed at the time when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was digging the trench around Madinah. That is because some of the believers asked permission due to necessity, while the hypocrites would leave without asking permission. So Allah, Exalted, excluded those who do not ask permission from the category of the believers. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to give permission to the believer whom necessity does not compel to detain, and he is "whom he wills." Then He commanded him to seek forgiveness for both categories of believers, those who were given permission and those who were not. In this there is reassurance for the believers and kindness toward them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 63–64:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among you like the call of some of you to others. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He already knows your state, and the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

This verse is addressed to all the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Allah the Exalted commanded them not to make their address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in calling him like the address of some of them to others, for their custom was to call one another by names, and that out of extreme rudeness and lack of regard. So Allah the Exalted commanded them in this verse and in others that they should call the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by his most noble names, and that is what reverence and honouring require. Thus the one who seeks to call upon him should say: "O Messenger of Allah," and this should be with reverence, lowered voice, and piety, and not follow their habit of addressing one another in this manner. This was said by Mujahid and others.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the meaning of this verse is only: "Do not consider the Messenger's supplication against you to be like the supplication of some of you against others," i.e., his supplication against you is answered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording of the verse rejects this meaning, and the first is more correct.

(p-415) Then Allah the Exalted informed them that He knows those among them who slip away, concealing themselves. "Liwadh" (concealment and evasion) is the verbal noun of "lawadha," not of "ladha," for it was said of it "liyadhan," as mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others.

Then He commanded them to beware of the punishment of Allah the Exalted and His vengeance if they oppose His command. The Exalted's saying ﴿who oppose his command﴾ means: their opposition occurs after His command. This is like when you say: "the rain came from a wind," where "from" (ʿan) indicates what goes beyond a thing. "Fitna" in this context means: afflictions and calamities in this world, or the painful punishment in the Hereafter, and the hypocrites must have one of these two.

The Exalted's saying "Unquestionably" (alā inna) opens the speech and informs that Allah the Exalted has what is in the heavens and the earth, in ownership and in creation. Then He informed them that He already knows the state of the inhabitants of the earth and the heavens, and He specifically mentioned those addressed among them because that is the place of proof against them, and they are the ones I mean by it. As for His saying ﴿and the Day they are returned﴾, it may be that it is an object governed by His saying "He knows," and it may be that the implied meaning is: "and the manifest knowledge for you," or something similar, "on the Day," so the accusative is in the sense of a time adverb. The majority read "yurjaʿūn" with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the jīm, while Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu ʿAmr read "yarjiʿūn" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a kasra on the jīm.

ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir al-Juhani said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ reciting this verse, the closing of Surah al-Nur, and he said: 'Allah is Seeing of all things,'" and the rest of the verse is clear.

The commentary on Surah al-Nur is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 24, verses 63–64:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among you like the call of some of you to others. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He already knows your state, and the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

This verse is addressed to all the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Allah the Exalted commanded them not to make their address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in calling him like the address of some of them to others, for their custom was to call one another by names, and that out of extreme rudeness and lack of regard. So Allah the Exalted commanded them in this verse and in others that they should call the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by his most noble names, and that is what reverence and honouring require. Thus the one who seeks to call upon him should say: "O Messenger of Allah," and this should be with reverence, lowered voice, and piety, and not follow their habit of addressing one another in this manner. This was said by Mujahid and others.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the meaning of this verse is only: "Do not consider the Messenger's supplication against you to be like the supplication of some of you against others," i.e., his supplication against you is answered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording of the verse rejects this meaning, and the first is more correct.

(p-415) Then Allah the Exalted informed them that He knows those among them who slip away, concealing themselves. "Liwadh" (concealment and evasion) is the verbal noun of "lawadha," not of "ladha," for it was said of it "liyadhan," as mentioned by al-Zajjaj and others.

Then He commanded them to beware of the punishment of Allah the Exalted and His vengeance if they oppose His command. The Exalted's saying ﴿who oppose his command﴾ means: their opposition occurs after His command. This is like when you say: "the rain came from a wind," where "from" (ʿan) indicates what goes beyond a thing. "Fitna" in this context means: afflictions and calamities in this world, or the painful punishment in the Hereafter, and the hypocrites must have one of these two.

The Exalted's saying "Unquestionably" (alā inna) opens the speech and informs that Allah the Exalted has what is in the heavens and the earth, in ownership and in creation. Then He informed them that He already knows the state of the inhabitants of the earth and the heavens, and He specifically mentioned those addressed among them because that is the place of proof against them, and they are the ones I mean by it. As for His saying ﴿and the Day they are returned﴾, it may be that it is an object governed by His saying "He knows," and it may be that the implied meaning is: "and the manifest knowledge for you," or something similar, "on the Day," so the accusative is in the sense of a time adverb. The majority read "yurjaʿūn" with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the jīm, while Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu ʿAmr read "yarjiʿūn" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a kasra on the jīm.

ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir al-Juhani said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ reciting this verse, the closing of Surah al-Nur, and he said: 'Allah is Seeing of all things,'" and the rest of the verse is clear.

The commentary on Surah al-Nur is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.
